Lesson 1: The aircraft is only one part of the system

Course: Introduction to Drone Technology

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Identify the aircraft, control station, command link and payload.

Lesson

A client asks for a map of a small construction site. Before choosing a drone, write down the result the client needs: a dated visual record, a measurable surface, or an inspection finding. These are different products. A sharp photograph does not automatically provide reliable measurements, and a model that looks complete can still contain gaps.

Think in four connected parts. The aircraft carries the equipment. The remote pilot station allows the crew to monitor and direct it. The command link carries instructions and status. The payload collects the useful information. The people, procedures and operating environment determine whether these parts can work together safely. A camera specification alone cannot describe mission capability.

A multirotor can hold position and inspect a small area from different directions, but carrying more mass affects its performance. A fixed-wing aircraft generally suits sustained forward travel; its launch, recovery and turning needs must fit the site. A hybrid combines operating modes with additional system complexity. These are selection considerations, not promises about a particular model.

Separate three questions in every equipment comparison: Can it collect the required information? Can the crew operate it within the relevant limitations and permissions? Can the team check and deliver usable results? Automation can help execute a planned path. It cannot establish that the path is safe, lawful, or suitable for the data product.

For the construction request, produce a short equipment decision with assumptions. If the client has not defined accuracy, inspection criteria, or output format, record those as questions rather than selecting the most expensive aircraft.

Desk exercise

Create a four-part system diagram for a fictional construction survey. Add one failure consequence and one verification step for each part.

Marking guide

A strong answer links aircraft, control station, command link and payload to the client deliverable. It distinguishes capture capability from permission and validation, and identifies missing client requirements.

Reflection

Name one assumption you would verify before applying this lesson to a real project. Identify the source or competent person who could resolve it.

Consult the source register and the course review dependencies. The narrative and fictional scenarios are original instructional drafts. No source text or commercial examination item is reproduced. Regulatory and operational details require current-source mapping before approval.

pages.name: 01 · Understand the complete aircraft system
pages.html:

01 · Understand the complete aircraft system

A drone service is a chain of dependencies, not a camera that happens to fly. The aircraft produces motion; the control station presents information and accepts commands; the command-and-control link connects them; the payload measures or records the subject. People, procedures, batteries, positioning services and the operating environment support that chain. A failure in any supporting element can invalidate a mission even when the aircraft remains airborne.

Separate commands from observations. A command requests an action; telemetry reports what a sensor or system believes is happening. A displayed battery percentage is an estimate, not a promise of remaining flight time. A map icon is a calculated position, not independent proof that the aircraft is where the operator expects. Cross-check important information using an appropriate independent cue, such as direct observation, a consistent instrument indication or a documented ground reference.

Describe an aircraft using capabilities, limitations and evidence. State what payload it carries, what deliverable it supports and which manual establishes its limits. Do not infer approval to operate from a product feature. Before selecting equipment, write the intended output, site constraints and acceptance tests. That turns a catalogue comparison into a defensible system decision.

Worked example

A client asks for a construction map. A high-resolution camera may supply sharp photographs, but a measurable surface also needs suitable capture geometry, a reference system, control or independent checks, processing and an accuracy report. The aircraft purchase alone does not meet that requirement.

Your exercise

Draw the aircraft, station, link and payload for a fictional mapping service. For each, name an input, an output and one failure consequence. Add the person responsible for checking it.

Model answer and reasoning

Aircraft: receives control demand and produces motion; propulsion failure threatens containment. Station: receives telemetry and displays status; a frozen display can mislead the pilot. Link: carries commands/status; interruption requires the approved contingency. Payload: receives scene information and produces files; missing files can invalidate delivery. The pilot and data lead assign and verify these checks before accepting the job.

Knowledge checks

Does a telemetry value independently prove the physical situation?

No. It is a system estimate that needs an appropriate cross-check.

What should be defined before equipment selection?

The required deliverable, constraints and evidence of acceptance.

Further reading / verification

  • FAA-PHAK: aircraft systems and aeronautical decision-making; aircraft-specific operating manual

pages.name: 02 · Choose an aircraft and payload for the job
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

02 · Choose an aircraft and payload for the job

Multirotors can hold position and change viewing direction without maintaining forward flight. Fixed-wing aircraft generate lift primarily through airflow over a wing and need an operating concept compatible with launch, recovery and turning. Hybrid aircraft combine flight modes and introduce transition considerations. These are design tendencies, not performance guarantees. Compare the actual aircraft manual and the permitted operating environment rather than assuming one type is universally better.

Payload selection begins with the measurement. RGB imagery records visible appearance. A thermal sensor measures radiance in a spectral band and needs interpretation and suitable conditions. A ranging sensor produces distance observations that depend on calibration, positioning and geometry. A heavier payload changes the aircraft system; it may affect endurance, balance, integration and authorised configurations.

Use a decision matrix with must-have requirements separated from preferences. A platform that fails a mandatory requirement is not rescued by a high total score. Record uncertainty: if a supplier cannot establish a required accuracy or integration capability, mark it unresolved. A small pilot project with explicit acceptance criteria is more useful than an unsupported claim of survey-grade results.

Worked example

For a compact roof inspection, the ability to observe detail from controlled viewpoints may matter more than covering a very large area. For a long corridor, coverage efficiency matters, but launch/recovery, airspace and operating permissions can eliminate an otherwise attractive aircraft.

Your exercise

Compare two fictional aircraft against five requirements: output type, spatial detail, site footprint, payload integration and evidence of operating limits. Identify one disqualifying requirement.

Model answer and reasoning

An acceptable matrix names the deliverable and uses evidence for each rating. A missing approved payload configuration is a stop condition, not a low preference score. The recommendation explains tradeoffs and includes a trial to verify image quality or measurement performance before a commercial promise.

Knowledge checks

Can payload mass be evaluated independently of the aircraft?

No. It affects the integrated system and its limitations.

Should a mandatory failure be averaged into a score?

No. Mandatory constraints are pass/fail gates.

Further reading / verification

pages.name: 03 · Power, positioning and information quality
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

03 · Power, positioning and information quality

A battery supplies finite stored energy. Voltage, current, temperature and condition affect what can be delivered under load. Energy in watt-hours is nominal voltage multiplied by amp-hours; this is useful for comparing stated capacities, but it does not establish usable flight endurance. Usable energy depends on the aircraft, payload, weather, battery condition and required reserve. Use manufacturer procedures for charging, storage, inspection and retirement.

Position estimates combine sensors and algorithms. GNSS can be degraded by poor geometry, reflections, interference or obstruction. An inertial system estimates motion from accelerometers and gyroscopes but accumulates error without suitable correction. A compass is vulnerable to magnetic influences. Extra satellites or an RTK status label do not guarantee a correct datum, clean observations or accurate delivered coordinates.

Information quality has several dimensions: accuracy, precision, completeness, freshness and traceability. A very repeatable wrong position is precise but inaccurate. A correct coordinate with no reference system is incomplete. A recent firmware update without a configuration record weakens traceability. Preserve raw observations, record system versions and validate critical results against independent evidence.

Worked example

A nominal 22.2 V battery rated at 5 Ah represents 111 Wh. Two packs with that label need not provide the same usable endurance after ageing or under different loads. Plan from approved performance evidence and reserve policy rather than dividing a marketing flight-time figure into the job.

Your exercise

Calculate nominal energy for a 14.8 V, 6 Ah pack. Then list four reasons this calculation cannot predict a safe mission duration.

Model answer and reasoning

The nominal energy is 88.8 Wh. Actual load, battery condition, temperature and required reserve all matter; so do the aircraft/payload configuration and environmental conditions. The calculation is a capacity comparison, not permission to exhaust the pack or a substitute for the manual.

Knowledge checks

What is the nominal energy of 14.8 V × 6 Ah?

88.8 Wh.

Can a precise position be inaccurate?

Yes. Repeated measurements can cluster around an incorrect location.

Further reading / verification

  • MANUFACTURER: battery care and positioning limitations

pages.name: 04 · Build and verify a complete mission workflow
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

04 · Build and verify a complete mission workflow

A repeatable workflow links discovery, planning, capture, processing, validation and delivery. At discovery, turn the client's question into a concrete output and acceptance criterion. At planning, verify permissions, site constraints, roles, equipment and contingency arrangements. At capture, follow the approved operational process and collect evidence that the required coverage and file integrity were achieved.

Processing is not the final quality gate. Check whether the data answer the original question and whether the limitations are clear. Missing coverage, a wrong reference system or an unsuitable thermal observation cannot always be repaired by software. Retain an issue log and decide whether to reprocess, recapture or qualify the deliverable. Do not quietly fill evidential gaps with confident language.

Use versioned handover folders with a readme explaining dates, units, reference systems, methods and known limitations. Keep original files separate from working exports and final deliverables. Close the workflow by recording what the client accepted and what should change next time. This learning loop improves reliability without erasing the evidence of an imperfect result.

Worked example

A visually attractive orthomosaic has a blank area behind a structure. If the client's question concerns that area, the output fails even when the rest looks excellent. Record the gap and agree on a permitted recapture or a clearly limited delivery.

Your exercise

Write a one-page workflow for a fictional site progress record with an acceptance checklist and a file handover structure.

Model answer and reasoning

Include the client question, date/area to be covered, operational approval gate, capture quality checks, file verification, processing version and a final coverage review. Handover separates originals, working files and finals; the readme records limitations. Acceptance explicitly addresses coverage and the intended decision, not merely file count.

Knowledge checks

Is processing success the same as client acceptance?

No. The result must satisfy the agreed purpose and quality criteria.

What should happen to a known data gap?

Record it and agree on recapture or a qualified deliverable.

Further reading / verification

  • FAA-PHAK: decision-making; project-specific data specification

Lesson 1: Understand the motion before using the controls

Course: Drone Flight Fundamentals

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Describe aircraft axes and basic motion.

Lesson

Use a simulator for this lesson. Keep propellers removed from any aircraft used only for desk familiarisation. The purpose is to connect control input, aircraft attitude and movement, not to teach an unsupervised first flight.

An aircraft has longitudinal, lateral and vertical axes. Roll, pitch and yaw describe rotation about those axes. Position describes where the aircraft is; attitude describes its orientation. They are related but different. A multirotor can change its attitude before a clear positional change becomes visible, so a pilot who reacts only to displacement may respond late.

In a simplified stationary hover, the upward component of thrust balances weight. Tilting the thrust vector introduces a horizontal component. If total thrust does not increase, its vertical component becomes smaller. This explains why a demand for horizontal acceleration also needs performance margin to maintain height. It does not provide a universal control setting: flight controllers and aircraft designs implement control differently.

Orientation changes the pilot's visual interpretation. A simulated aircraft facing the pilot makes a leftward aircraft motion appear on the opposite side of the pilot's viewpoint. Start by describing the aircraft's own orientation aloud. Avoid guessing from the screen location alone. A camera view and a map are useful aids, but they are not interchangeable with direct aircraft attitude awareness.

Before a simulator exercise, agree a starting state, exercise boundary, instructor intervention signal and stop condition. Afterwards compare intended movement with actual movement. Record one observation, its possible cause and the next controlled practice step. Better practice reduces uncertainty instead of rewarding a lucky recovery.

Desk exercise

In a simulator, annotate three screenshots showing roll, pitch and yaw. Explain one difference between aircraft-relative and pilot-relative directions.

Award credit for correct axes, separation of attitude and position, and a defined stop condition. Do not assess physical flight competence from screenshots.

pages.name: 01 · Forces, axes and the meaning of control
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

01 · Forces, axes and the meaning of control

Describe roll about the longitudinal axis, pitch about the lateral axis and yaw about the vertical axis. These are rotations of the aircraft, not necessarily directions of travel. A multirotor can point one way while translating another way. Distinguish attitude, heading, track and groundspeed when describing what a display or observer is showing.

In a simplified level hover, the vertical component of total thrust balances weight. Tilting the thrust vector creates a horizontal component; maintaining the same vertical support then requires greater total thrust. This explains why manoeuvring and wind compensation can consume performance margin. The simplified relationship T cos(theta) = W describes the geometry; it is not a flight command or a full model of a particular controller.

Weight, aerodynamic forces and control authority interact with the environment and payload. Knowing the names of forces does not establish a safe operating limit. Use the aircraft manual and supervised training for actual control inputs. The desk exercise here asks you to explain a response, not to practise unapproved manoeuvres outdoors.

Worked example

If an idealised vehicle has weight 100 N and tilts 30 degrees while maintaining vertical equilibrium, total thrust would need to be about 115.5 N because cos(30°) ≈ 0.866. A real aircraft also has aerodynamic and control effects not captured by this model.

Your exercise

Sketch the weight vector, tilted thrust vector and its vertical/horizontal components. Explain why heading and track may differ in wind.

Model answer and reasoning

Weight acts downward; the thrust vector follows the simplified aircraft thrust direction. Its vertical component must support weight and its horizontal component changes motion or opposes a disturbance. Heading describes orientation; track describes movement over the ground, so wind and control choices can make them differ.

Knowledge checks

Which axis is associated with yaw?

The vertical axis.

Does tilting leave the vertical thrust component unchanged?

No. At the same total thrust it reduces the vertical component.

Further reading / verification

  • FAA-PHAK: principles of flight and aerodynamics; MANUFACTURER: control modes

pages.name: 02 · Orientation, reference frames and control modes
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

02 · Orientation, reference frames and control modes

Control interpretation depends on the reference frame. A direction on a hand controller may be tied to the aircraft heading, an earth reference or a special assisted mode. Never infer the active frame from the aircraft's appearance alone. Identify the actual mode, its indications, the sensors it requires and its fallback behaviour from the manual.

Orientation errors arise when a pilot confuses their own viewpoint with the aircraft's axes. In a simulator, start with a stable reference and introduce one change at a time. Describe what you expect before applying an input, observe the result and pause when prediction and observation disagree. This separates learning from random correction.

Assistance is conditional. Position holding, obstacle sensing and automated return functions depend on valid inputs and suitable conditions. Sensor coverage may have blind regions; maps and height references may be wrong or out of date. A mode change can alter workload abruptly. Build a mode-awareness briefing that states what is available, how loss of an assistance function is recognised and where the approved response is documented.

Worked example

A simulated aircraft faces towards the operator. An aircraft-relative right movement appears opposite to the operator's own right. The lesson is reference-frame awareness, not a universal instruction for a particular product's control mapping.

Your exercise

For a simulator configuration, record three modes, the reference frame of each, its required sensors and one indication of a mode change.

Model answer and reasoning

A good table cites the actual simulator/manual configuration and distinguishes heading-relative from earth-relative behaviour. It states the sensor dependencies and a visible mode annunciation. It avoids assuming that a mode name has the same meaning across manufacturers.

Knowledge checks

Should a mode name be assumed identical across products?

No. Verify the specific manual and configuration.

What should follow an unexpected simulator response?

Pause, reconcile the reference frame/mode and restart at an appropriate difficulty.

Further reading / verification

  • MANUFACTURER: mode descriptions, limitations and fallback indications

03 · Normal procedures and simulator briefing

A briefing should define a task, boundaries, roles, expected sequence and stop criteria. A checklist verifies essential conditions; it does not replace understanding. Distinguish a challenge-response check from a memory aid and document who has authority to stop the exercise. For this course, practical manoeuvring remains in a suitable simulator or approved training environment.

Use a progression from stable attitude/orientation awareness to controlled transitions between simple tasks. Add only one workload factor at a time. Record the simulator model, assistance settings and success criteria, because a change in configuration can make two sessions incomparable. A successful exercise is one the learner can explain and repeat, not a lucky outcome.

Before each scenario, state the normal indications and what would make the scenario invalid. A poor frame rate, unexpected control mapping or missing instructor communication can prevent meaningful learning. Stop and resolve those conditions rather than recording a misleading pass. After the scenario, compare the intended and observed sequence using a concise event log.

Worked example

04 · Abnormal events, prioritisation and debrief

An abnormal scenario changes a normal assumption: information may be unreliable, a function unavailable or workload excessive. Recognise the change, protect control and containment priorities, communicate as appropriate and use the aircraft/operator's approved procedure. Generic online lessons cannot supply one correct lost-link, battery or positioning response for all aircraft.

In desk-based rehearsal, work through indications, competing explanations and the evidence needed to distinguish them. Avoid premature diagnosis. A moving map anomaly might originate in position data, display behaviour or an incorrect reference; a symptom is not automatically a component failure. Identify which actions require immediate execution under the approved procedure and which diagnostic work belongs after the aircraft is safe.

A useful debrief separates the timeline, observations, decisions and outcomes. Ask what information was available at the time rather than judging solely from hindsight. Record a corrective action with an owner and a verification method. Repeating the scenario at the same difficulty without addressing its cause is not a learning plan.

Worked example

In a simulator, the map display freezes while other indications continue. The learner identifies unreliable information, follows the approved simulation procedure and records the discrepancy. They do not invent a live-aircraft emergency command from this example.

Your exercise

Create a four-column debrief for a fictional positioning anomaly: observation, interpretation, decision and evidence to review. Include an action for the next simulation.

An acceptable debrief distinguishes the frozen display from a proven navigation failure, records the information available at each decision and cites the applicable procedure. The follow-up tests recognition and communication after correcting the training/configuration issue; it does not reward a speculative diagnosis.

Knowledge checks

Is a symptom proof of a diagnosis?

No. Several causes can produce similar indications.

What makes a corrective action useful?

A clear owner, a change to make and evidence that verifies improvement.

01 · Translate a story into a capture plan

A useful image has a purpose within a sequence. Identify the audience, the intended message and the action or understanding the work should support. A property overview, a progress record and a cinematic narrative use different viewpoints and editing logic. Write the story before proposing aircraft movements.

A shot list describes subject, framing, duration, relationship to other shots and the operational dependencies of capture. Establishing views orient the audience; medium views connect elements; details support specific information. Plan transitions so that direction, time and place remain understandable. A beautiful isolated shot may not belong in the final sequence.

Separate creative intention from operational feasibility. Record permissions, privacy concerns, access and conditions for each proposed view, and let the authorised operating process determine what can be captured. Prepare alternatives that preserve the narrative without pressuring a crew to deliver an unsuitable manoeuvre.

Worked example

A fictional farm film needs to explain the relationship between fields, a river and access routes. An establishing view provides context, a medium view shows activity and a detail provides texture. The sequence should not imply that unrelated views are adjacent.

Your exercise

Write a six-shot storyboard for a fictional site overview. Give each shot a narrative purpose and a feasible alternative.

Model answer and reasoning

The storyboard moves from context to relationship to detail, uses consistent direction and explains why each shot belongs. Alternatives preserve the same information without requiring a particular flight. The plan records constraints rather than assuming creative approval authorises capture.

Knowledge checks

Does a visually impressive shot necessarily help the story?

No. It needs a purpose in the sequence.

Can a creative brief override operational constraints?

No. Feasibility and authorisation remain separate gates.

02 · Exposure, motion and image detail

Exposure describes the amount of light recorded and the sensor response. Shutter time affects motion depiction; aperture, where adjustable, affects light and optical behaviour; ISO changes the image-processing/sensitivity setting and noise tradeoffs. The controls available and their useful ranges depend on the camera. Avoid universal settings that ignore scene brightness, movement and intended output.

For moving imagery, shutter time interacts with frame rate and the visual appearance of motion. A creative convention is not an operational rule. For measurement imagery, sharpness and stable geometry may take priority over cinematic motion blur. Check actual files at the detail needed for the intended use, not only the small live display.

Focus, lens condition, compression, lighting and subject movement also affect usable detail. More pixels do not recover blur or lost highlights. Record a short camera test, inspect representative material and choose settings for the deliverable. Do not change aircraft handling to rescue an unsuitable camera plan without an operational review.

Worked example

Two photographs have the same pixel dimensions. One is blurred by motion and the other retains edges needed for an observation. Equal resolution labels do not make them equally useful. A test image should be checked against the required detail.

Your exercise

For a fictional progress photograph and a cinematic clip, list the different image priorities and a verification test for each.

Model answer and reasoning

The progress image prioritises interpretable detail, comparable views and appropriate exposure. The clip prioritises intended motion appearance and continuity while remaining usable. Both use camera-specific controls and representative file review; neither assumes a single shutter setting works for every scene.

Knowledge checks

Can more pixels repair motion blur?

No. Pixel count is only one aspect of usable detail.

Should cinematic settings automatically be used for mapping?

No. The deliverable has different image-quality priorities.

  • Camera-specific exposure/focus/recording documentation

03 · Capture continuity and preserve the originals

Continuity lets the audience understand changes in viewpoint and time. Record direction of movement, lighting, subject state and camera settings where they affect the sequence. For repeat progress views, give viewpoints stable identifiers and record how they were obtained, while respecting the approved operating method.

Capture quality checks should happen while a permitted remedy is still possible. Verify that required views exist, files can be read and representative material has suitable detail/exposure. A thumbnail or file count does not prove complete coverage. If a required view is unavailable, record the gap rather than silently substituting a misleading one.

Preserve original media and distinguish it from proxies, working edits and exports. Use a naming and backup process appropriate to the project, verify transfers and retain a clear association between the shot list and files. Protect personal or client information during transfer and review. Do not erase the only source copy because an export appears to play correctly.

Worked example

A monthly view labelled N-01 is obstructed on one visit. A different angle can be supplied as an alternative, but it should receive an appropriate identifier and a note explaining that it is not a directly comparable replacement.

Your exercise

Create a shot-to-file register with six planned views, capture status, file references, continuity notes and a transfer-verification field.

Model answer and reasoning

Every planned view has a status, including unavailable or qualified results. File references distinguish original media from edits. Continuity notes record relevant changes, and transfer checks confirm readable files rather than relying solely on copy completion. The register preserves evidence of missing coverage.

Knowledge checks

Does a completed copy operation prove every file is usable?

No. Use appropriate integrity and readability checks.

Should an unavailable repeat view be silently replaced?

No. Label the alternative and its comparability limitation.

  • Camera media-handling documentation; project data-handling plan

04 · Edit, review and deliver a coherent sequence

Editing selects and orders evidence for the intended story. Build an assembly from the storyboard, then remove shots that do not help the audience. Maintain spatial and temporal clarity. Music, graphics and colour treatment should support the message without disguising a material limitation or implying an observation the source does not support.

Review the output against the brief and technical delivery requirements. Check readability, audio rights/levels where relevant, titles, aspect ratio and representative playback. Export settings depend on the target; a large master and a delivery copy may serve different needs. Keep the project and source associations needed for later corrections.

Use a structured client review with version identifiers and consolidated feedback. Distinguish an error from a new creative request or scope change. Before publication, confirm the appropriate rights and privacy arrangements. Deliver a concise readme and the agreed files, with any unavailable views or other material qualifications visible.

Worked example

A client wants both a widescreen presentation and a vertical social clip. Reframing may remove important context, so the vertical version needs its own review rather than an automatic crop treated as equivalent.

Your exercise

Create an edit review checklist and handover index for a fictional 60-second site film with two aspect ratios.

Model answer and reasoning

The checklist covers narrative clarity, continuity, exposure/colour consistency, titles, rights and target playback. Each aspect ratio is checked for retained context. The index identifies versions, approved outputs and source/project retention arrangements, while new requests are recorded through change control.

Knowledge checks

Is a vertical crop always equivalent to the master?

No. Reframing can remove necessary context.

How should new creative requests be handled?

Separate them from errors and agree on any scope/time/price change.

Learning focus

Distinguish a visual model from a validated measurement product.

Lesson

A project manager asks whether a stockpile has grown since last month. A visual model can show its shape, but a volume comparison requires a consistent boundary, reference surface, coordinate system and method. Begin with the decision the measurement will support and the tolerance needed. Do not select settings from the word mapping alone.

Ground sampling distance describes the approximate ground size represented by a pixel under stated geometry. It is not the same as positional accuracy. Blur, weak geometry, calibration, control quality, surface texture and processing choices can all affect the delivered result. A fine-looking raster does not establish survey-grade performance.

Control points help relate a model to a reference frame. Independent checkpoints are withheld from that adjustment and used to assess performance. If every surveyed point is used to fit the model, the residuals at those fitted points cannot serve as an independent test. Record point roles before processing and keep their measurement provenance.

Horizontal and vertical references must be stated. A height may refer to an ellipsoid or to a local height system; mixing them can create a systematic offset. Record coordinate units and the transformation used, including any required grid files or assumptions. On-screen alignment is insufficient evidence of a correct transformation.

For the stockpile scenario, define the same base surface and boundary rules for both dates, inspect coverage, and report uncertainty and exclusions alongside the change. A delivery note should let another analyst understand what was measured and what remains uncertain.

01 · Define a measurable product and its reference system

A map, model and measurement report answer different questions. An orthomosaic supports a plan-view representation, a surface model represents the visible surface and a terrain model aims to represent terrain under a specified definition. Vegetation, structures and occlusion affect what can be established. Define the product and its use before capture.

Coordinates require a reference system, units and relevant epoch/height information. Assigning a CRS tells software how to interpret existing values; transforming coordinates computes values in another reference. Labelling incorrect coordinates with the desired CRS does not transform them. Horizontal and vertical references must be considered separately.

An accuracy specification describes the quantity, method and acceptance criterion to be evaluated. Ground sample distance describes represented ground spacing per pixel; it is not a guarantee of positional accuracy. Write a quality plan with independent checks, coverage and limitations so that the delivered number is interpretable rather than simply visually convincing.

Worked example

A dataset in degrees is relabelled as a metre-based CRS without transformation. Its values now have an incorrect meaning; changing the label did not move them correctly into the target system. Verify the source definition before choosing a transformation.

Your exercise

Draft a specification for a fictional site surface product, naming the intended decision, horizontal/vertical references, units and independent acceptance evidence.

Model answer and reasoning

The specification distinguishes surface from terrain, states the coordinate/height definitions and explains what independent observations will test the result. It treats GSD as image sampling, identifies coverage/occlusion limits and avoids calling an output survey-grade without an appropriate specification and evidence.

Knowledge checks

Is assigning a CRS the same as transforming coordinates?

No. Assigning defines interpretation; transformation computes new coordinate values.

Does small GSD guarantee positional accuracy?

No. Accuracy depends on the whole measurement and validation chain.

Further reading / verification

  • QGIS 3.44 documentation: layer/project CRS and transformations; USGS calibration guidelines

02 · Design capture geometry and usable image quality

Photogrammetric reconstruction depends on observations of common scene features from suitable viewpoints. Coverage, overlap, viewing geometry, surface texture, lighting and image sharpness all affect the result. A flight pattern alone cannot guarantee reconstruction in feature-poor, reflective, moving or occluded areas.

Use the camera geometry to understand sampling. In a simplified nadir, flat-ground model, GSD is approximately height above the local ground multiplied by sensor pixel pitch, divided by focal length, with consistent units. Terrain changes alter the local height relationship. This geometric estimate is not an accuracy assessment or a universal flight-height instruction.

Plan quality checks for representative images and difficult areas. Check focus, blur, exposure, coverage and consistency, and identify where additional suitable views may be needed under an approved operation. The required geometry should follow the product specification and camera/processing guidance rather than a single overlap percentage copied into every project.

Worked example

With a fictional 2.4 μm pixel pitch, 8 mm focal length and 80 m local height, the simplified GSD is 0.024 m, or 2.4 cm/pixel. A different local terrain height changes the estimate; independent checks are still needed for accuracy.

Your exercise

Calculate simplified GSD at 60 m with the same fictional camera. Identify three site conditions that can invalidate an otherwise neat capture plan.

Model answer and reasoning

The estimate is 0.018 m, or 1.8 cm/pixel. Poor texture, reflective/moving surfaces and occlusion can undermine reconstruction; blur and exposure also matter. The result is a sampling calculation, not an operational recommendation or proof of accuracy.

Knowledge checks

What units must be consistent in the GSD formula?

Height, pixel pitch and focal length must use compatible length units.

Is one overlap percentage suitable for every project?

No. Geometry, scene and product requirements vary.

03 · Separate control, checkpoints and model fitting

Control observations help establish or constrain a model. Checkpoints test the resulting model independently. Using the same observations for fitting and then presenting their residuals as an independent accuracy test confuses these roles. Record point identities, reference definitions, measurement methods and how each point is used.

Consider distribution, not just count. A cluster of checkpoints in one easy corner cannot establish performance everywhere else. Evaluate horizontal and vertical results as relevant to the product, with attention to terrain, edges and difficult surfaces. A small test set or uncertain reference observations limit the strength of any claim.

Keep residuals and uncertainty concepts distinct. A residual is a difference under a specified comparison; an uncertainty statement concerns the measurement process and its limitations. Report the signs, units, summary statistics and scope of the checks. An excellent fitting score is useful diagnostic information, but it is not a substitute for independent validation.

Worked example

For fictional checkpoint vertical differences +0.03, −0.04 and +0.05 m, RMSE is √((0.0009+0.0016+0.0025)/3) ≈ 0.0408 m. Three points are used only to teach the calculation, not to satisfy an accuracy standard.

Your exercise

Calculate mean signed error and RMSE for fictional differences +0.02, −0.02 and +0.04 m. Explain what these statistics do not establish.

Model answer and reasoning

The mean signed error is about +0.0133 m; RMSE is about 0.0283 m. These describe this tiny sample and reference comparison. They do not establish full-site accuracy, a particular confidence level or compliance with a standard without an appropriate sampling/design and reference-quality assessment.

Knowledge checks

Can fitting residuals alone be called independent validation?

No. The test observations need to be independent of fitting.

Why does checkpoint distribution matter?

It affects which parts and conditions of the product are actually tested.

04 · Process, inspect and report measurement limitations

A processing record should preserve input identities, software/version, important settings, coordinate handling and quality decisions. Inspect alignment and coverage before investing in downstream outputs. A successful job status or plausible surface can hide local artefacts, gaps and reference errors.

Validate the final delivered product, not only an intermediate model. Reprojection, clipping, resampling or export can introduce new issues. Check units, extents, orientation, height reference and representative values in an independent viewing environment where practical. Maintain links between the report, checkpoints and the exact output version.

Report what the product supports and where it is limited. Distinguish measured surface, inferred/filled areas and unobserved regions. Supply a concise methods/quality note and avoid implying a professional survey certification unless that service is within the provider's competence and applicable authority. A reproducible limitation is more valuable than an unqualified accuracy slogan.

Worked example

A surface passes an intermediate check but is exported with a different height interpretation. The delivery check catches a consistent offset. The corrected output and report receive a new version so the recipient can identify the change.

Your exercise

Write a processing and final-QA checklist for a fictional orthomosaic/surface delivery, including one failure that requires recapture rather than reprocessing.

Model answer and reasoning

The checklist records inputs/settings/references, tests alignment and coverage, evaluates independent checks and rechecks final exports. Missing usable observations behind an occlusion may require an authorised recapture; software cannot establish a surface it never observed. The report identifies inferred areas and qualified use.

Knowledge checks

Why test the exported product?

Export and transformation can change the delivered result.

Can processing always recover unobserved surfaces?

No. Inference or filling is not equivalent to observation.

Lesson 1: Sell a defined outcome with visible assumptions

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Learning focus

Convert a client request into a scoped work order.

Lesson

A client asks for a roof inspection tomorrow and requests a fixed price immediately. A useful commercial response starts with scope. Ask what decision the inspection must support, which structures are included, what defects matter, and whether a qualified specialist must interpret the imagery. Capturing images and certifying a roof condition are different responsibilities.

Separate the work into preparation, capture, analysis and delivery. Preparation includes confirming access, operational feasibility, crew availability and required permissions. Capture depends on appropriate equipment and conditions. Analysis includes image review and traceable observations. Delivery includes agreed files, a reporting format and a review window. Omitting these stages from a quote does not remove their cost.

List assumptions that can change the work: access restrictions, weather, incomplete site information, additional structures, repeat attendance or a new reporting requirement. State who can authorise a scope change. A low initial price with an undefined deliverable creates disputes even when the flying is technically successful.

Define acceptance in terms the client can check. Examples include a complete agreed asset list, an image index, explicit limitations and the stated report format. Avoid promising that no defects exist merely because none were visible. Keep observed evidence separate from interpretation and from work outside the operator's competence.

Finish with a handover that explains naming, retention, permitted sharing and follow-up. Use fictional client information in the exercise. This course does not replace jurisdiction-specific operational approval, professional certification or a reviewed commercial contract.

pages.html:

01 · Discover the client decision and scope the work

A commercial brief should describe the decision the client needs to make, not merely the aircraft they want flown. Ask who will use the result, what action it supports and what evidence will make it acceptable. A marketing image, an inspection observation and a measurement product require different methods and review skills.

Write the scope as deliverables, coverage, quality criteria, responsibilities and exclusions. Record site access, permissions, client-supplied information and the dependencies that can delay work. A request for survey accuracy needs a defined reference system, accuracy specification and validation method; do not substitute a sharp-looking image for those requirements.

Confirm the brief in writing before pricing. Ambiguous words such as complete, accurate or all defects should become testable statements. If the information needed to quote is missing, propose a discovery stage or conditional estimate. A scope boundary protects both parties by making the promised service understandable.

Worked example

A property owner requests a roof survey. Discovery reveals that the intended decision is whether a contractor should inspect a suspected leak. The deliverable becomes dated imagery and located observations, with interpretation by the appropriate specialist, rather than an unsupported structural certification.

Your exercise

Rewrite “drone survey of our warehouse” into a scope with three acceptance criteria and two exclusions.

Model answer and reasoning

Specify the site/area, capture date, required views and an observation index. Acceptance can require agreed coverage, readable detail and a documented handover. Exclude inaccessible/occluded areas and professional engineering certification unless separately contracted and competently provided. Record approval and access dependencies.

Knowledge checks

What should discovery identify first?

The client decision and evidence needed to support it.

Why define exclusions?

They prevent an ambiguous request becoming an unsupported promise.

pages.name: 02 · Plan delivery around operational dependencies
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

02 · Plan delivery around operational dependencies

Commercial scheduling must respect the operational decision, not the reverse. A confirmed booking does not resolve airspace, land access, crew competence, weather or aircraft availability. Build an approval and dependency register showing the owner, evidence, expiry and consequence of each unresolved item.

Separate commercial authority from operational authority. A client can approve a budget without authorising a flight. Define who makes the operational go/no-go decision and how a postponement is communicated. A contract should not reward the crew for ignoring a stop condition.

Plan the data workflow alongside the fieldwork. Identify file transfer, processing time, quality review and specialist interpretation needs before promising delivery. Establish alternatives for conditions that prevent the intended observation. An alternative must still answer the client question; simply flying another route may not recover an unsuitable thermal or measurement observation.

Worked example

A construction manager agrees on a date but cannot confirm access to a critical area. The dependency remains open. The delivery plan records who will resolve it and when the job must be rescheduled rather than treating the booking as operational clearance.

Your exercise

Create a dependency register for a fictional two-day job with access, airspace information, weather, crew and data-processing entries.

Model answer and reasoning

Each entry has an owner, required evidence, decision deadline and effect on delivery. It distinguishes permissions from commercial sign-off and identifies the operational decision-maker. The schedule includes validation and an agreed response if the data needed for acceptance cannot be collected.

Knowledge checks

Does a booking authorise flight?

No. Operational requirements are separate.

What makes an alternative capture plan acceptable?

It remains authorised and produces evidence suitable for the original decision.

Further reading / verification

  • Approved operator procedures; current site/airspace information

pages.html:

03 · Price effort, uncertainty and change

A sustainable price starts with a cost model: labour, equipment allocation, travel, processing, review, insurance/overheads and delivery support. Define which costs vary with the job and which must be recovered across the business. Quoting only the time airborne hides much of the effort.

Distinguish markup from margin. Markup divides gross contribution by cost; margin divides it by selling price. In a simplified model, a selling price for target gross margin m is cost divided by (1 − m). This is an illustrative pricing calculation, not a market rate or tax recommendation. Use applicable tax and professional advice for actual invoices and contracts.

Price uncertainty transparently. State assumptions, what constitutes a scope change and how approval happens before extra work. A contingency allowance is not permission to ignore foreseeable dependencies. Track estimates against actual effort so that future prices reflect evidence rather than memory.

Worked example

For fictional direct costs of R4,000 and a target 20% gross margin, the simplified price is R5,000, not R4,800. R800 added to R4,000 is a 20% markup but only a 16.7% margin. Taxes and other costs are excluded from this exercise.

Your exercise

Calculate the price for fictional costs of R6,000 at a 25% gross margin. List three assumptions that should accompany a quote.

Model answer and reasoning

R6,000 ÷ 0.75 = R8,000 before any applicable taxes or excluded costs. Assumptions should address coverage/access, capture conditions and processing/delivery requirements. Changes require an agreed scope, price/time impact and explicit approval; they are not quietly absorbed or billed afterwards.

Knowledge checks

Are markup and margin identical?

No. Their denominators differ.

When should scope changes be approved?

Before the extra work, with the effect on price and timing clear.

Further reading / verification

  • Original illustrative cost model; project contract and qualified tax advice where applicable

pages.html:

04 · Handover, acceptance and recurring value

Handover should make the work usable without the client having to reconstruct your process. Supply the agreed outputs, a concise readme, observation or measurement limitations and a clear route for questions. File names, dates, units, reference systems and version identifiers should be consistent.

Acceptance checks the agreed criteria, not an expanding informal wish list. Record whether each criterion is met, qualified or outstanding, with evidence. If a limitation prevents the intended decision, agree on the remedy or a revised acceptance; do not bury the issue in a large archive.

Recurring work creates value when repeated observations are comparable. Preserve capture references, processing settings and known differences between visits. A visually different result may reflect changed conditions or methods rather than physical change. Close each job with a review of estimates, defects, client questions and improvements, then obtain appropriate permission before using project imagery in marketing.

Worked example

A monthly progress record uses consistent view identifiers. One visit has an obstructed viewpoint; the handover marks it unavailable and explains the consequence instead of inserting a different view under the old name.

Your exercise

Create an acceptance sheet for a recurring progress service with a change log and a client handover index.

Model answer and reasoning

The sheet lists coverage, date, view identifiers, output formats and limitations. It records exceptions and agreed remedies, preserves a method/change log and separates originals, working data and final outputs. Acceptance and any marketing permission are distinct decisions.

Knowledge checks

Does visual difference always mean site change?

No. Capture or processing differences can cause it.

Is marketing reuse implied by delivery?

No. Establish the appropriate permission and purpose separately.

Lesson 1: Increase complexity one variable at a time

Course: Advanced Flight Techniques

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Build a simulator progression from simple to complex tasks.

Lesson

Advanced performance is repeatable decision-making under a defined workload. It is not a collection of dramatic manoeuvres. Begin with a simulator baseline that the learner can complete consistently: stable orientation, a simple path and a deliberate stop. Document the conditions so the next exercise is comparable.

Increase only one demand at a time. A route can become more complex, a camera task can be introduced, or a simulated wind condition can change. Changing everything together prevents the instructor from identifying why performance deteriorated. A successful outcome after an uncontrolled recovery is not evidence of a reliable method.

Describe margins explicitly. Aircraft performance, attention, available space and time to respond are finite. A task that uses nearly all attention for framing may leave little capacity for monitoring warnings. More automation can change workload rather than simply reducing it. The crew still needs to understand what mode is active and what the aircraft will do when the plan changes.

For each exercise, define a normal completion criterion and an interruption criterion. The learner should be able to explain when to stop without treating that decision as failure. Record errors by observable behaviour: delayed recognition, incorrect mode assumption or an incomplete cross-check. Avoid vague judgements such as bad flying.

A progression plan should end with an instructor review of evidence, not a self-issued operational qualification. Real aircraft exercises require the appropriate training environment, instructor, permissions and aircraft-specific procedures. This opening lesson remains a desk and simulator activity.

Design three simulator exercises that add one demand each. Include a stop condition and a measurable debrief question for every exercise.

Marking guide

Credit controlled progression and measurable behaviour. Reject plans that rely on unapproved real-world proximity flying or treat a simulator result as operational authorisation.

pages.html:

01 · Performance margins before complexity

An advanced task combines demands that may each be manageable alone: position control, orientation, observation, communication and payload operation. Performance margin is the capacity left after meeting current demands. It can shrink through fatigue, unfamiliarity, environmental complexity or degraded assistance even when the aircraft remains within a published limit.

Build prerequisites from observable evidence. A learner should demonstrate the simpler component skills consistently in the intended simulator configuration before combining them. A previous flight count or confident self-description does not establish readiness. State the required supervision and approvals for any subsequent real operation.

Use a task-demand table to identify coupling. If a payload adjustment requires looking away from traffic information at the same moment a mode change increases control workload, those demands interact. Reduce or sequence them before adding complexity. Advanced practice should improve judgement about when not to continue, not normalise operating at the edge of control.

Worked example

A simulated inspection requires the learner to navigate, frame a close detail and answer a radio prompt simultaneously. The instructor first separates the tasks, then introduces communication at a low-demand moment before increasing complexity.

Your exercise

List five demands in a simulated inspection and mark the two most likely to compete for attention. Propose a change that removes one conflict.

Model answer and reasoning

A strong answer identifies control/orientation and payload framing as potentially competing, with communication and monitoring adding demand. Assigning a payload role or sequencing the framing task can reduce conflict. The proposed exercise still requires clear stop criteria and evidence of the prerequisite skills.

Knowledge checks

Does experience count alone prove readiness?

No. Readiness needs current, observable evidence.

What is an effective response to coupled workload?

Reduce, assign or sequence demands before increasing difficulty.

Further reading / verification

  • FAA Risk Management Handbook: risk management and human performance

pages.name: 02 · Plan coordinated movement in simulation
pages.html:

02 · Plan coordinated movement in simulation

A planned camera move describes the desired path, orientation and framing over time. These are separate variables. A smooth-looking result can hide unstable control or an unnecessarily narrow margin. Use a simulator to decompose the move into entry, stable portion and exit, and to identify where workload changes.

Choose reference features that support orientation without encouraging fixation. A learner who watches only the subject may stop noticing aircraft attitude, boundaries or other relevant cues. Describe a deliberate monitoring pattern and the conditions that require pausing the simulation. Do not generalise an attractive cinematic manoeuvre into a recommended live-aircraft technique.

Evaluate the process as well as the image. Record whether the learner anticipated the next phase, maintained situational awareness and ended the manoeuvre within the exercise bounds. Variation should come from planned practice conditions, not repeated improvisation. If the control system or assistance setting changes, re-establish the baseline before comparing performance.

Worked example

For a virtual orbit, separate path consistency from camera pointing. First rehearse each component, then combine them at a simple pace with defined entry/exit references. The simulation result says nothing by itself about authorisation to orbit a real structure.

Your exercise

Create a three-phase plan for a simulated tracking shot. For each phase, identify the control demand, visual reference and observation to record.

Model answer and reasoning

The plan defines an entry reference and settled configuration, a stable section with an intentional monitoring pattern, and an exit with sufficient room in the virtual exercise. It records path and framing separately and has a pause condition for lost orientation or conflicting cues.

Knowledge checks

Are path and framing the same variable?

No. Evaluate them separately before combining them.

What risk does subject fixation create?

Other control, boundary and situational cues can be missed.

  • Approved simulator syllabus and aircraft operating documentation

pages.name: 03 · Rehearse a complex mission as a crew
pages.html:

03 · Rehearse a complex mission as a crew

A complex mission needs a shared picture of the task, responsibilities and changing conditions. Brief the operating concept, who monitors each critical source of information and the language used to stop or replan the exercise. A crew member should be able to raise a concern without solving it first.

Rehearse handovers explicitly. State what is being transferred, the current state and the acknowledgement that completes the transfer. Silence is not acceptance. Where one person performs several roles, identify when those roles cannot be fulfilled simultaneously and redesign the task. Adding another person without a clear role can increase ambiguity rather than reduce workload.

Inject a small number of defined changes into a desk or simulator scenario. Useful changes include a lost client requirement, a conflicting information update or a role becoming unavailable. The objective is to observe the team's decision process, not to surprise people with impossible combinations. Keep a timeline so that the debrief can distinguish a communication failure from a missing plan.

Worked example

A virtual mission's payload operator becomes unavailable. The crew pauses the scenario and removes the payload task rather than silently assigning it to a pilot already handling a demanding phase. The revised plan is read back before restarting.

Your exercise

Write a two-person simulation briefing with responsibility boundaries and a handover phrase. Add a contingency for one person becoming unavailable.

Model answer and reasoning

The briefing names the pilot/control role and the information/payload role, defines a stop phrase and requires explicit acknowledgement for transfers. The contingency reduces or stops the task when role coverage becomes inadequate. It does not assume that spare attention is always available.

Knowledge checks

Is silence an adequate acknowledgement of a handover?

No. Transfer must be explicitly acknowledged.

Does more crew automatically mean less risk?

No. Roles and communication have to be designed.

Further reading / verification

  • FAA-PHAK: crew resource management and aeronautical decision-making

pages.name: 04 · Evaluate readiness and build the next practice cycle
pages.html:

04 · Evaluate readiness and build the next practice cycle

Readiness is a decision supported by a defined standard and repeatable evidence. An attractive output, a single successful attempt or the absence of an incident does not establish competence. Evaluate control, awareness, communication, procedure use and decision-making in addition to the visible product.

Use a rubric before watching the performance. Separate critical failures from areas that can improve through ordinary practice. A task performed with an unrecognised boundary excursion should not receive a pass because the final image looks good. When evidence is insufficient, record that result rather than forcing a numerical score.

Turn the debrief into a focused next session. Select one or two specific improvements and choose an exercise that exposes them without unnecessary complexity. Record the conditions and the expected evidence. A competent instructor decides whether simulator learning transfers to approved practical training; this self-study course does not issue an advanced-flight rating.

Worked example

A learner produces a smooth simulated shot but misses two required monitoring calls. The result is a communication/awareness gap, not a complete pass. The next session isolates the monitoring task at lower control demand.

Your exercise

Design a readiness rubric with four criteria and one non-negotiable stop/fail condition. Explain how an insufficient-evidence result would be handled.

Model answer and reasoning

Criteria can cover orientation/control, monitoring, communication and procedure use. A loss of exercise containment or an unacknowledged control transfer can be critical. Insufficient evidence leads to a specifically planned reassessment, not a guessed score or an unsupported statement of live-flight competence.

Knowledge checks

Does no incident equal demonstrated competence?

No. Observe performance against explicit criteria.

Who determines practical training transfer?

A competent instructor within the applicable approved training framework.

Further reading / verification

  • Approved training assessment standards; FAA Risk Management Handbook

Course: Weather and Airspace Management

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Distinguish forecast, observation and site evidence.

Lesson

A weather forecast is a prediction for a place and period. An observation describes conditions at its reporting point and time. A site observation describes what the crew can currently see or measure nearby. These sources complement each other, but none automatically describes every part of the operating area.

Consider a site beside a ridge and large buildings. A regional wind forecast may not capture the local flow around those features. Combine the evidence with aircraft limitations and the operation's approved procedures. Define when the crew will reassess and what conditions require stopping. Avoid converting an illustrative classroom wind value or distance into a universal operating rule.

pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

01 · Read weather as time-and-location evidence

Weather information has a source, observation or validity time, location and purpose. An observation reports conditions at a place/time; a forecast describes expected conditions over a stated period/area. Neither automatically describes every point of a mission site. Check the publication time and the period relevant to the planned work.

Local terrain, buildings, surfaces and changing heating can alter conditions. A calm observation elsewhere does not establish calm airflow around a structure. Distinguish measured information from assumption and identify what site assessment or specialist input is needed. Use approved operational limits and current aviation weather services rather than a generic consumer icon as the sole decision basis.

Keep a weather evidence register with the source, time, applicability and unresolved concerns. Plan reassessment points because conditions and forecasts change. This lesson develops interpretation and decision records; it does not give universal wind, visibility or cloud limits for your aircraft or operation.

Worked example

A forecast covers the wider region during the job, but a local building corridor may produce different airflow. The crew records the forecast as one input and assesses site conditions through the approved process instead of treating the regional value as a guarantee.

Your exercise

Create a weather evidence register for a fictional morning job and identify what would trigger reassessment.

Model answer and reasoning

The register distinguishes observations and forecasts, records validity/location and links each concern to the mission. Triggers include changed site conditions, new warnings, expired information or a delayed capture window. The decision uses applicable approved limits, not an invented universal threshold.

Knowledge checks

Does a forecast prove the exact site condition?

No. Its spatial/temporal applicability and local effects matter.

Why reassess after a delay?

The relevant weather and information validity may have changed.

Further reading / verification

  • FAA Aviation Weather Handbook: observations/forecasts and local effects; current official aviation weather service

pages.name: 02 · Connect weather to aircraft and data performance
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

02 · Connect weather to aircraft and data performance

Weather affects aircraft performance, crew workload and the usefulness of collected data. Wind changes the relationship between motion through the air and motion over the ground; temperature and air density influence performance; precipitation and moisture may exceed equipment limitations. Use the aircraft/payload documentation for actual limits and approved decision rules.

A simple wind-vector exercise helps separate heading, track, airspeed and groundspeed. It is a learning model, not a flight plan. Real operations must account for the aircraft's control system, performance, airspace and contingencies. Do not infer a safe return plan from a single averaged wind value.

Weather can also invalidate the measurement even when flight is otherwise feasible. Illumination, cloud movement, surface wetness and thermal conditions can affect comparability or interpretation. The operational go decision and the data-quality go decision both need to be satisfied. Record why the conditions suit the particular observation.

Worked example

In a simplified straight-line example, an air-relative speed of 8 m/s with a 3 m/s headwind gives 5 m/s groundspeed; a 3 m/s tailwind gives 11 m/s. This arithmetic omits real aircraft/mission effects and does not establish endurance or reserve requirements.

Your exercise

Use a fictional 6 m/s air-relative speed and 2 m/s headwind to calculate groundspeed. Then identify two data-quality reasons to postpone a capture.

Model answer and reasoning

The simplified groundspeed is 4 m/s. Rapid illumination changes may undermine comparable RGB observations, and unsuitable thermal/environmental conditions may undermine the intended thermal interpretation. The actual postpone decision follows the measurement specification and approved operational process.

Knowledge checks

Can safe-to-fly conditions still produce unsuitable data?

Yes. The intended measurement has its own conditions.

Does a vector exercise establish a safe reserve?

No. It is a simplified conceptual calculation.

Further reading / verification

  • FAA Aviation Weather Handbook: weather/performance; MANUFACTURER: environment limits

03 · Build an airspace and information-validity picture

Airspace assessment is a current, location-specific task. Identify the planned area, altitude reference, time window, relevant airspace/locations and the authoritative information needed. Static charts, amendments, supplements and current notices have different roles. A familiar map or a previous approval is not automatically applicable to a new operation.

Record which permissions and coordination are required through the applicable operator/authority process. Do not infer permission from the absence of a warning in a consumer application. Land access, airspace authority, pilot privileges and operator approvals address different questions and must not be substituted for each other.

Track the information lifecycle. Note when a source was checked, the effective period and any conditions or expiry. If a notice is ambiguous or the planned activity does not match the permission, resolve it before proceeding. The course uses fictional scenarios rather than prescribing current frequencies, routes or local operating permissions.

Worked example

A team has access to a site but discovers that an information update affects the intended time window. Land access does not resolve the airspace issue. The mission remains unconfirmed until the relevant authority/operator process resolves the conflict.

Your exercise

Create an information/permission register for a fictional project with separate rows for land access, airspace, pilot privileges and operator scope.

Model answer and reasoning

Each row identifies the authority/source, applicability, effective time, owner and evidence needed. No row is used as a substitute for another. Open questions and conditions remain visible, with a decision deadline before work is treated as operationally feasible.

Knowledge checks

Does an application’s silence equal permission?

No. Verify the applicable authoritative requirements.

Is land access the same as airspace authorisation?

No. They concern different permissions.

  • SACAA Aeronautical Information: AIP/AIC/NOTAM resources; current operator approval process

pages.name: 04 · Make and communicate a defensible decision
pages.html:

04 · Make and communicate a defensible decision

A decision brief combines current evidence, applicable limits, uncertainty and alternatives. State what is known, what remains unresolved and who has authority to decide. A deadline or travel cost is a commercial consequence, not evidence that conditions are acceptable.

Choose explicit reassessment points and stop conditions. A no-go can become a revised plan if the new plan is authorised and still meets the client's evidence need. Do not quietly expand limits or reinterpret a permission to preserve the original schedule. Communicate the decision and its operational and delivery consequences to the relevant people.

After the job or rehearsal, compare the observed conditions with the plan and record useful changes. A good outcome does not prove every decision was sound; an inconvenient cancellation can be a well-supported professional decision. The capstone evaluates the quality of the information and reasoning rather than rewarding a predetermined go answer.

Worked example

A capture window moves beyond the validity of the information used in the briefing. The team pauses and reassesses instead of treating the original go decision as permanent. The client receives a clear explanation of the delivery effect and alternatives.

Your exercise

Write both a go-with-conditions and a no-go brief for two fictional variations of the same job, stating what evidence changes the decision.

Model answer and reasoning

Both briefs name the evidence, applicable limits, authority and unresolved issues. Conditions are specific and reassessment is timed. The no-go explains the relevant uncertainty or failure and proposes an authorised alternative if one exists. Neither relies on pressure to meet the schedule.

Knowledge checks

Does a successful outcome validate every decision?

No. Review the evidence and reasoning available at the time.

Can schedule pressure change an approved operating limit?

No. Revise the plan or timing through the proper process.

Further reading / verification

  • FAA Risk Management Handbook; approved operator decision and briefing procedures

Lesson 1: Preserve the evidence before changing the system

Course: Drone Maintenance and Troubleshooting

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Separate a symptom from a diagnosis.

Lesson

A team reports intermittent vibration after replacing a propeller. The symptom is vibration under particular conditions. The recent replacement is relevant evidence, but it is not yet proof of the cause. Begin by recording the aircraft identification, configuration, part details, time of the change and when the symptom first appeared.

Follow the aircraft manufacturer's inspection and maintenance instructions. Do not improvise a live flight to reproduce an unexplained fault. A damaged or suspect propulsion component requires a safe stop and an appropriate technical review. Power down and isolate equipment according to its instructions before handling it. Battery damage, heat or swelling must be managed using the applicable manufacturer and site procedures.

Good troubleshooting changes one controlled variable at a time and states the expected observation. Record what was inspected, what was changed, who did it and what the result was. A software update, calibration or restart can alter the state and erase clues. Capture permitted diagnostic records first, without collecting unnecessary personal information.

Use a fault log with separate columns for symptom, evidence, hypothesis, test and result. A hypothesis can be rejected; that is useful progress. Replacing several parts together may restore operation but leave the cause unknown. Record that uncertainty honestly.

Return to service is a defined process with competent oversight, required checks and a record of release. This lesson teaches documentation and decision structure. It does not authorise repairs or override manufacturer limits.

Complete a fictional fault log for vibration after a component change, identifying three useful records and two unsupported assumptions to avoid.

Marking guide

A good log preserves configuration, separates cause from timing, uses approved instructions and states who may release the aircraft back to service.

01 · Inspection evidence and approved limits

Maintenance begins with identifying the exact aircraft, component and configuration. A procedure for a similar model is not necessarily applicable. Record serial numbers where relevant, operating time or cycles, software versions, the reported defect and the manual revision used. Separate routine preflight inspection from maintenance tasks requiring specific authorisation or competence.

An inspection compares an observed condition with an approved limit or requirement. Words such as fine or probably normal do not communicate that comparison. Describe location, extent and the method of observation, and retain suitable evidence. If the applicable limit cannot be established, the result is unresolved rather than automatically serviceable.

Respect isolation and handling instructions. Batteries, propellers, stored energy and automatic activation can create hazards on the ground. Follow the manufacturer's safety procedures and the operator's approved maintenance system; this course does not instruct a learner to open, energise or repair an aircraft. A desk-based defect record is useful precisely because it makes uncertainty visible before equipment is returned to use.

Worked example

A propeller has a visible mark near its root. A photograph alone cannot establish whether it meets an approved condition limit. Record the exact propeller identity, the mark's location and the applicable manual requirement, then use the authorised assessment path.

Your exercise

Complete a fictional defect record for an observed vibration, including identity, configuration, symptom, evidence and disposition.

Model answer and reasoning

The record identifies the aircraft and relevant components, states when vibration occurred and distinguishes observation from diagnosis. It records evidence and the manual reference, assigns an authorised reviewer and marks the equipment unavailable or unresolved until the applicable process determines disposition.

Knowledge checks

Is probably normal an inspection standard?

No. Compare evidence against an applicable documented requirement.
