02 · Distinguish symptoms from causes

A symptom is what was observed; a cause explains why it occurred. Several causes can produce a similar symptom, and several symptoms can share one cause. Begin with the event timeline and configuration rather than replacing the first component that comes to mind. Preserve logs and other evidence before a change destroys the original state.

Build a fault tree or hypothesis table. For each candidate explanation, state what evidence would support it, what would contradict it and whether checking it is authorised and safe. A useful test distinguishes hypotheses; a test that produces the same result for all candidates adds little information. Avoid repeated powering or flight tests on suspect equipment unless the approved process specifically permits them.

Software and configuration changes deserve the same discipline as hardware work. Record versions, settings and the time of any change. A correlation after an update is a starting point for investigation, not proof that the update caused the defect. Escalate with a concise reproduction history and evidence package rather than an unverified diagnosis.

Worked example

A system reports intermittent positioning warnings. Candidate explanations include environmental obstruction, interference, a configuration issue or a hardware fault. An authorised log review across locations may distinguish these better than immediately replacing a receiver.

Your exercise

Create a hypothesis table for intermittent image blur with three possible causes and one discriminating evidence check for each.

Model answer and reasoning

Candidates include movement/exposure, optical contamination/focus configuration and vibration. Image metadata and a controlled authorised ground inspection may distinguish them. The answer states what evidence would contradict each explanation and avoids proposing an unsafe flight as the first diagnostic step.

Knowledge checks

Does correlation prove the cause of a defect?

No. It supports a hypothesis that needs discriminating evidence.

What makes a diagnostic check useful?

It safely distinguishes competing explanations.

03 · Control changes and escalate effectively

A controlled change has a purpose, an authorised method, a known baseline and a verification plan. Change one relevant variable at a time when the approved process permits, so that the outcome can be interpreted. Record what was changed and retain the original evidence. Do not improvise an aircraft configuration or substitute an unapproved part to see what happens.

Escalation should reduce the receiving specialist's uncertainty. Include equipment identity, configuration, symptom timeline, conditions, steps already taken, exact messages and the desired decision. Separate raw evidence from your interpretation. Remove unnecessary personal or client data from shared logs while preserving the information needed for diagnosis.

Define ownership while an issue remains open. The equipment's operational status, the next action and the person who can authorise return to use should be unambiguous. If a workaround changes an operating assumption, it requires its own review; a temporary label does not make it safe or approved.

Worked example

A support ticket says the aircraft is unreliable. A useful escalation instead states the exact model/version, the warning sequence, the conditions and the authorised checks performed, with time-correlated logs and a clear serviceability question.

Your exercise

Write a concise escalation for a fictional intermittent telemetry fault. Include a baseline, evidence index and the decision you need.

Model answer and reasoning

The escalation separates the observed interruption from a claimed component fault, includes timestamps and configuration, lists approved checks and supplies a minimal evidence package. It asks whether further inspection, repair or restriction is required and identifies who owns equipment status while waiting.

Knowledge checks

Can a temporary workaround bypass configuration approval?

No. Its changed assumptions still require review.

Why separate raw evidence from interpretation?

It lets the specialist assess the observations without inheriting an unsupported diagnosis.

04 · Return-to-use evidence and reliability learning

A defect being cleared from a display is not by itself evidence of an acceptable return to use. The responsible authorised person needs a record of the defect, the action taken and the verification required by the applicable system. Verify that related records, configuration and any restrictions agree. Close the issue only when the defined acceptance evidence is present.

Reliability records make repeated defects visible. Track the relevant exposure measure, such as operating hours, cycles or deployments, alongside events. Ten events across ten operations differs from ten across a thousand. Do not combine unrelated definitions or compare periods with incompatible logging practices.

Use recurring evidence to improve inspection, training or escalation. A trend does not automatically justify a maintenance interval change; the approved maintenance system controls that decision. Preserve the audit trail and distinguish a proposed improvement from an approved instruction. The final exercise evaluates your documentation and reasoning, not your authority to certify an aircraft.

Worked example

Three similar warnings appear after a component change. Record exposure and configuration for each occurrence, compare the symptom definitions and refer the trend through the authorised process. Do not assume the replacement resolved the underlying issue.

Your exercise

Create a return-to-use checklist and a small reliability register with event, exposure, action, verification and owner fields.

Model answer and reasoning

The checklist requires traceable defect/action records, approved verification, correct configuration and an identified release authority. The register records consistent exposure and event definitions so that rates can be compared. A proposed process improvement remains marked pending approval until accepted by the responsible authority.

Knowledge checks

Is a cleared warning sufficient release evidence?

Not on its own; apply the approved verification and release process.

Why record exposure alongside defect counts?

Counts alone do not show how frequently defects occur relative to use.

This course concerns the United States FAA pathway. It does not establish South African privileges or cover every practical competence needed for a commercial service. 02 · Reason through operating rules and airspace

Rules questions often turn on applicability: who is acting, what aircraft/activity is involved, where it occurs and whether a particular approval or exception applies. Build a rule card with the current provision, its conditions and the evidence needed. Do not treat an anecdote about one operation as a general permission.

For airspace study, distinguish the class/structure, chart information, airport environment and current restrictions. A chart is interpreted with its legend, date and applicable publications. An electronic planning tool can assist, but a familiar interface does not replace understanding or provide every required authorisation.

Work a scenario in order: define the proposed operation and time, identify relevant airspace/restrictions, find the current rule, determine the required authorisation/coordination and record the conclusion. Keep US-specific procedures separate from ICAO-style radio practice and South African requirements. Where the information is incomplete, the correct study answer is to identify what must be resolved, not to invent a clearance.

Worked example

A fictional US task is near an airport and within controlled airspace. The learner identifies the relevant chart/class information and checks the current authorisation process before deciding feasibility. Permission from the property owner does not answer the airspace question.

Your exercise

Build a rule-and-airspace worksheet for two fictional US tasks with different locations/times. For each, identify the official source needed and the unresolved conditions.

Can property permission resolve controlled-airspace requirements?

No. Different permissions address different matters.

How should an incomplete scenario be handled?

Identify and resolve the missing information instead of assuming permission.

03 · Weather, loading and performance calculations

Weather knowledge connects observations and forecasts to aircraft capability and operational decisions. Read the relevant official weather material, practising the distinction between source time, validity and local applicability. A numerical limit is meaningful only when it applies to the aircraft and operation under consideration.

Loading and performance involve more than total mass. Configuration, centre of gravity where relevant, payload integration and environmental conditions affect capability. Use the aircraft documentation and the ACS learning objectives to identify what must be checked. Do not invent a generic centre-of-gravity limit or derive safe endurance from a marketing figure.

Practise unit discipline and explain what a calculation does and does not establish. A simple headwind subtraction can illustrate groundspeed, while real planning also needs an approved performance/contingency method. Keep a calculation sheet with units, assumptions and a reasonableness check. The goal is to reason from the scenario rather than memorise an isolated number.

Worked example

In an intentionally simplified example, 7 m/s air-relative speed and a 2 m/s direct headwind produce 5 m/s groundspeed. The result does not establish usable battery time or a safe return policy; those require aircraft- and operation-specific evidence.

Model answer and reasoning

The sheet uses consistent units and labels all values fictional. It separates nominal energy from usable endurance, groundspeed from airspeed and aircraft approval from arithmetic. It records load/configuration, environmental assumptions, reserve policy and the need for approved documentation rather than claiming the calculation authorises flight.

Knowledge checks

Is nominal energy the same as safe usable endurance?

No. Load, condition, environment and reserve requirements matter.

Should a calculation include assumptions and units?

Yes. Without them its meaning and validity are unclear.

01 · Understand the South African approval and training pathway

Begin with current SACAA licensing, training, examination and legislation sources. Terminology and applicable provisions have changed over time, so record the exact document, edition and checked date rather than relying on an old course title. This independent self-study course supports preparation; it is not an ATO approval, licence application or assurance that a particular applicant meets the requirements.

Separate the pilot, aircraft, operator and proposed operation. A pilot credential does not automatically authorise every aircraft or business activity. An operator approval does not establish that a particular pilot, configuration, site and mission are within scope. Build an evidence matrix showing the distinct questions and the current authority/source for each.

Confirm an intended training provider's approval and scope through current SACAA information. Keep examination, radiotelephony, language, medical and practical-assessment questions in a personal pathway checklist for verification with the appropriate approved provider. Do not substitute this course's self-study completion for a required external assessment.

Worked example

A fictional learner has a pilot document but wants to offer a new specialist service. The approval matrix records aircraft/operator/mission-scope questions separately; it does not mark the entire business authorised because one document exists.

Your exercise

Create a current-source pathway checklist and a four-column pilot/aircraft/operator/mission matrix. Mark all applicant-specific requirements as needing verification.

Model answer and reasoning

The checklist cites current SACAA entry points and records provider/authority confirmation, document edition and open questions. The matrix distinguishes privileges and approvals rather than treating them as interchangeable. Required practical or licensing assessments remain external, with no invented eligibility finding.

No. The relevant external process remains required.

02 · Aircraft knowledge and human performance foundations

Aircraft understanding connects systems, forces, limitations and information quality. Review the supplied aircraft/principles notes and the actual operating manual. Explain the relationship between control input, system response and observed evidence without assuming assistance functions are available under every condition.

Human performance affects information gathering and decisions. Workload, fatigue, expectation and fixation can narrow attention or encourage premature conclusions. Use a briefing that identifies responsibilities, uncertain information and a clear route to stop or replan. Self-assessment should identify a concern rather than rationalise it away to meet a schedule.

Practise reasoning with a paired scenario: first describe normal assumptions, then change one condition such as a degraded information source or unavailable crew role. Explain what needs reassessment and where the approved response is documented. Avoid teaching one universal emergency action for all aircraft. The exercise evaluates recognition and use of evidence, not practical competence.

Worked example

A fictional positioning indication becomes inconsistent with other observations. The learner identifies unreliable information and consults the applicable approved procedure instead of assuming a universal control input from an online example.

Your exercise

Build a systems-dependency map and a human-performance brief for a fictional observation job. Include a change that requires reassessment.

Model answer and reasoning

The map connects aircraft, station, link, positioning and payload with their limitations. The brief allocates monitoring and decisions, names workload concerns and stop language, and identifies the approved procedure source. It distinguishes symptom recognition from an unsupported diagnosis or practical flight instruction.

Knowledge checks

Can assistance functions be assumed available in every condition?

No. Their dependencies and limitations must be understood.

What should a degraded information source trigger?

Recognition, appropriate approved priorities and reassessment of the plan.

03 · Integrate weather, navigation and communications

Weather, position/reference information and communication describe different parts of the same mission picture. Review the supplied subject notes and use current official information for the actual site/time. Identify where a forecast applies, how a coordinate or height is referenced and which communications process is required under the approved operation.

A navigation statement without units or a reference can be ambiguous. Distinguish heading from ground track, altitude references from local height, and a planned position from independent evidence of an actual position. Do not supply real operational routes or frequencies from a generic training exercise.

Communication should preserve a shared understanding of identity, state, restrictions and next action. Practise structured information and explicit clarification in the radiotelephony course, but verify local procedures with a competent instructor and current SACAA material. A confident voice is not evidence that a message is correct. When a critical instruction is unclear, resolve it rather than inventing the missing detail.

Worked example

A fictional brief gives a height but not its reference, and a changed capture time falls outside the weather information used. The learner identifies both ambiguities before deciding feasibility and does not assume that a radio acknowledgement resolves them.

Your exercise

Write a combined information brief with weather validity, position/height references, communications responsibilities and two clarification questions.

Model answer and reasoning

The brief uses time/location-specific sources, explicit units/references and named communication roles. Questions resolve the missing height definition and the delayed weather applicability. It distinguishes information exchange from operational authorisation and preserves unresolved restrictions.

Knowledge checks

Does confident delivery make a message correct?

No. Content, references and restrictions must be verified.

What is missing from an unreferenced height?

Its datum/reference and context, which can materially change its meaning.

Course: BVLOS Operations

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Explain how losing direct visual observation changes safety assumptions.

Lesson

This is a conceptual, desk-based introduction. It does not authorise BVLOS operations or provide a flight procedure. Work with a fictional mission and keep all approval, aircraft capability and crew qualification questions unresolved until supported by the appropriate authority and competent specialists.

In a basic visual operation, direct observation helps the crew understand aircraft position and surrounding hazards. Write a fictional BVLOS concept with five safety functions, a failure question for each, and named evidence required before approval review.

01 · Define the operating concept before choosing technology

Beyond-visual-line-of-sight study begins with an operating concept, not a range specification. Describe the purpose, area, time, aircraft/system, people, environment and how the proposed operation differs from a visual operation. Identify the assumptions normally supported by direct observation and what evidence would be needed when those assumptions change.

Technology does not establish permission. A long-range link, an automated route or a map display does not by itself address all air/ground risk, containment, oversight and approval requirements. Keep the applicable authority/operator process separate from the technical concept.

Use a desk-based concept of operations to expose missing evidence. Define boundaries and interfaces, including the people or services the operation depends on. Do not treat this introductory course as an approved BVLOS procedure or authority to conduct a real flight. The objective is a reviewable concept and a clear record of what cannot yet be justified.

Worked example

A fictional pipeline observation service proposes a long corridor. The concept identifies where direct observation would be unavailable, nearby third-party activity and the dependence on communications and contingency arrangements. A supplier's range claim is only one input.

Your exercise

Write a concept-of-operations outline with purpose, area/time, system, roles, dependencies and unresolved approval questions. Assign review responsibilities.

Model answer and reasoning

The outline defines the intended operation and changed assumptions, separates technical capability from authority and identifies evidence needed for air/ground risk and containment. It does not prescribe an unapproved route, separation method or real-world emergency action.

Knowledge checks

Does long advertised range grant BVLOS authority?

No. Capability and operational authorisation are separate.

What should an introductory BVLOS concept reveal?

Assumptions, dependencies, boundaries and evidence gaps.

pages.name: 02 · Analyse links, navigation and containment dependencies
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

02 · Analyse links, navigation and containment dependencies

Command-and-control, navigation and payload-data links may have different purposes and failure effects. Losing a video feed is not necessarily the same event as losing command/control, and a position estimate can degrade while a link remains connected. Define each interface and the information it carries before evaluating a failure.

Containment concerns where the aircraft could go under relevant conditions, not only the intended route line. Consider system behaviour, navigation uncertainty, environment and the applicable approved contingency concept. Claims require aircraft/system-specific evidence; a generic geofence feature is not a complete containment assurance.

Map common dependencies. Two apparently independent links may share power, antennas, coverage, a service provider or a control station. A redundancy label is only meaningful when the independence and failure handling are established. Record what is assumed, what has been tested and what remains for specialist assessment.

Worked example

A fictional primary and backup link use different radios but share one power source and one control computer. The dependency map shows that a common failure may defeat both, so the word redundant alone is not an adequate assurance.

Your exercise

Draw a dependency map distinguishing command/control, navigation and payload data. Add two common-cause failures and the evidence needed to assess them.

Model answer and reasoning

The map names the information and function of each path, identifies shared power/computation/services and separates loss-of-information effects. It asks for system-specific behaviour, verification and approved contingency evidence rather than assuming a generic automatic return function solves every failure.

Knowledge checks

Is payload video loss always command-link loss?

No. Distinguish functions and failure effects.

What makes a redundancy claim meaningful?

Evidence of independence and the system’s handling of relevant failures.

Further reading / verification

  • Aircraft/link safety documentation and approved operating concept

pages.name: 03 · Build an assurance argument and contingency evidence plan
pages.html:

03 · Build an assurance argument and contingency evidence plan

An assurance argument links a claim to evidence through explicit reasoning. For example, a proposed containment claim needs defined conditions, system behaviour and suitable verification, not only a statement that the aircraft has a feature. Identify the scope and limitations of each evidence item.

Use a hazard analysis to consider what could happen, the causes, existing controls and the remaining uncertainty. A control must be implemented, effective under the relevant conditions and assigned an owner. Do not multiply optimistic assumptions into an appearance of safety. Where the evidence is insufficient, record the claim as not yet justified.

Contingency planning belongs within the approved system and authority framework. In this course, write the information and test questions an authorised specialist must resolve; do not invent live-aircraft response sequences. Review who detects a condition, who decides, how communications are maintained and how the outcome is verified in an appropriate test environment.

Worked example

A claim that the operation remains contained after a navigation anomaly requires more than a geofence screenshot. The argument identifies the aircraft behaviour, dependencies, relevant conditions and approved verification evidence that would support or limit the claim.

Your exercise

Create an assurance table with three claims, supporting evidence, assumptions, gaps and a responsible reviewer.

Model answer and reasoning

Each claim is bounded and traceable. Evidence is specific to the system and operation, assumptions are explicit and gaps remain open until resolved. The reviewer role is proposed, not falsely recorded as having approved the work. Contingency details refer to the applicable approved procedure/test plan.

Knowledge checks

Is a feature list a complete assurance argument?

No. Show how relevant evidence supports a bounded claim.

What should happen to unsupported claims?

Keep them unresolved and identify the evidence/review needed.

Further reading / verification

  • Applicable authority safety/approval framework; approved system test and contingency documentation

pages.html:

04 · Review the concept through desk and simulator exercises

A review exercise tests whether the operating concept is understandable and whether people recognise when its assumptions fail. Brief the scope, roles and evaluation criteria. Use fictional information and a suitable simulator or tabletop format; no real BVLOS operation is authorised by the exercise.

Inject one meaningful change at a time and record the response. Examples include unavailable coordination, inconsistent information or a dependency losing its assumed independence. Evaluate recognition, communication, use of the approved framework and the decision to stop or revise. An exercise should reveal evidence gaps rather than pressure participants to keep the original plan alive.

Close with a decision record stating what the concept can support, what remains unproven and the next authorised review step. Separate successful rehearsal from regulatory approval or demonstrated aircraft safety. The completed self-study dossier is an input to competent specialist discussion, not an operational clearance.

Worked example

A tabletop exercise removes a service assumed by the concept. The team identifies which safety claims depend on it, records that they are no longer justified and suspends the proposed activity pending review rather than improvising a replacement in real time.

Your exercise

Prepare a tabletop exercise with roles, two sequential injects, observation criteria and a final unresolved-evidence register.

Model answer and reasoning

The exercise makes assumptions visible, records detection and decisions, and does not reward continuation after a key claim fails. Its debrief separates communication/process findings from system proof and assigns the next review/evidence tasks without inventing an approval.

Knowledge checks

Does successful rehearsal equal operational approval?

No. Those are different forms of evidence and authority.

What is a good response when a key assumption fails?

Recognise its effect, stop or revise through the approved review process.

01 · Select a measurement for an industry decision

Specialised work begins with a decision that ordinary imagery may not resolve. An infrastructure owner may need located visual observations; an agronomist may need a repeatable crop measurement; a maintenance team may need thermal evidence under defined conditions. Name the decision-maker and the evidence they consider valid before selecting a payload.

Distinguish observation from diagnosis. A visible pattern or unusual sensor value can direct further investigation without identifying a cause. Review the scale, timing, access, calibration and specialist interpretation needed. A sensor with a sophisticated name does not remove those dependencies.

Build a method suitability statement: what the method can observe, under which conditions and with which limitations. If the decision requires information the proposed method cannot establish, change the method or scope. Do not promise that one flight can answer every question about a structure, field or asset.

Worked example

A client asks whether a solar installation has an electrical fault. A thermal observation may identify an area for investigation, but a defensible diagnosis also depends on suitable conditions, measurement practice and qualified interpretation.

Your exercise

For three fictional client questions, identify a candidate sensor, the needed validation and the specialist who should interpret the result.

Model answer and reasoning

The answer connects sensor output to the actual decision and states its limits. It distinguishes RGB observation, thermal radiance/temperature interpretation and geometric measurement. Each proposal includes conditions and an appropriate independent or specialist check rather than assuming automatic diagnosis.

Knowledge checks

Does an anomalous value establish its cause?

No. It is evidence to interpret and corroborate.

What comes before payload choice?

The decision and its evidence requirements.

  • Manufacturer measurement documentation; project specialist specification

pages.name: 02 · Interpret thermal and agricultural observations cautiously
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

02 · Interpret thermal and agricultural observations cautiously

Thermal cameras observe radiation, and displayed temperature depends on the measurement model and conditions. Emissivity, reflected radiation, distance and the environment can matter. A colour palette is a display choice, not a diagnosis. Use the specific sensor instructions and competent thermography practice before making temperature claims.

Agricultural imagery also requires context. A spectral difference can reflect several influences, including crop state, soil/background, illumination or processing. Compare observations collected under a justified method and use relevant ground evidence. A vegetation index is not a universal yield, disease or nutrient diagnosis.

Preserve the acquisition conditions and processing choices. When comparing dates, identify changes in illumination, sensor configuration and scene conditions. If these undermine comparability, state the limitation rather than treating every difference as physical change. Avoid universal capture thresholds or interpretation rules that are not supported for the particular task.

Worked example

Two roof images use different automatic thermal scales. The colours look different, but this alone does not establish a temperature change. Compare actual measurement settings and conditions, with appropriate expertise.

Your exercise

Write an observation record for a fictional thermal anomaly and a separate crop-pattern observation, with alternative explanations and follow-up evidence.

Model answer and reasoning

Record time, conditions, sensor/configuration, location and the observed pattern. Thermal interpretation considers emissivity/reflection and display scale; crop interpretation considers capture comparability and ground evidence. Both records identify alternatives and a qualified follow-up instead of asserting a cause.

Knowledge checks

Does a palette colour prove a fault?

No. Display and measurement context matter.

Is a vegetation index a universal diagnosis?

No. Interpret it with suitable context and ground evidence.

  • FLIR: emissivity/reflected temperature guidance; sensor-specific radiometric calibration documentation

pages.name: 03 · Quantify infrastructure and volume with appropriate checks
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

03 · Quantify infrastructure and volume with appropriate checks

A measurement product must define what is being measured, its units, reference surface and uncertainty. A stockpile volume is the difference between a represented surface and a chosen base within a boundary. Changing that base or boundary can change the result even when the photographs are unchanged.

Visual infrastructure observations need location and traceability. Use an asset identifier, observation identifier, view reference and confidence/limitation statement. A blurred or occluded feature should not be classified with the same certainty as a clearly observed one. Specialist standards govern any professional condition assessment.

Validation must be independent of model fitting. Checkpoint observations used to assess accuracy should not also be used as control for that same assessment. Report the relevant checks, distribution and limitations rather than relying only on a software quality score. The final number is useful when the recipient understands its definition and how it was tested.

Worked example

For a simplified 100 m² area with mean height 2 m above an agreed flat base, the illustrative volume is 200 m³. Real surfaces and boundaries need a suitable method; this arithmetic does not validate a photogrammetric stockpile survey.

Your exercise

Define a fictional stockpile measurement: boundary, base, units, independent checks and an uncertainty/limitation statement. Explain the comparison basis.

Model answer and reasoning

The definition states the physical surface and base used, explains boundary selection and records the coordinate/height reference. Independent checks are withheld from fitting. The report distinguishes the calculated result from its validation and identifies occlusion, base assumptions or missing evidence.

Knowledge checks

Can fitting control serve as independent validation of the same model?

No. Independence would be lost.

Why specify the volume base?

The base is part of the definition and can materially change the result.

  • USGS calibration guidelines; USGS lidar specification: control/checkpoint separation

pages.html:

04 · Write a specialist-ready case report

A case report links the client question to the method, observations, checks and next decision. Provide a short summary and a traceable evidence index so that specialists can examine the supporting material. Keep assumptions and limitations close to the conclusions they affect.

Use consistent observation categories without implying greater certainty than the method supports. If a classification requires specialist judgement, identify who made it and under which scope. A data capture provider should not silently take responsibility for a conclusion outside their competence.

Close the loop with a review of usability. Can the recipient locate the observation, understand the conditions and decide what further action is justified? Corrections should be versioned and communicated. A professionally cautious report is not an unhelpful report: it states what is known, why it matters and what evidence would resolve what remains uncertain.

Worked example

An observation index links asset A-03, image I-17 and a marked location. The summary describes the observed feature and recommends specialist review, with the visibility limitation stated alongside it. The recipient can locate the supporting view without guessing.

Your exercise

Draft a one-page report for a fictional asset observation with three indexed findings, one unresolved issue and a proposed next step.

Model answer and reasoning

Each finding has an asset/location reference, evidence link, observation and confidence/limitation. The unresolved issue is not disguised as a negative finding. The next step names the evidence or specialist assessment needed and the report avoids unsupported safety or diagnostic certification.

Knowledge checks

Where should a limitation appear?

Close to the finding or conclusion it affects.

What makes a report specialist-ready?

Traceable observations, clear methods and conditions, and an explicit interpretive scope.

01 · Identify stakeholders, purpose and information harm

Ethical planning asks who may be affected by a capture, not just who commissioned it. People appearing in images, neighbouring occupants, workers, land managers and downstream users may have different interests. Identify the legitimate purpose, the information actually needed and the harms that could follow collection or disclosure.

Data minimisation is a design decision. Adjust coverage, timing, detail, retention and distribution to collect what the task requires rather than everything technically possible. A flight permission and a data-processing justification are different matters. Consult current South African privacy requirements and qualified advice where necessary; this course does not establish a legal basis for a particular project.

Record the decision process. A stakeholder map and purpose statement help the team notice unnecessary capture and challenge a client's vague request. If the purpose changes, reassess the data use instead of assuming the original arrangement covers every future use.

Worked example

A property marketing brief does not require a detailed view into neighbouring gardens. The team can frame the intended building while reducing unnecessary collection and separately reviewing any identifiable information in the output.

Your exercise

Map four stakeholders in a fictional school-roof observation project. Propose three ways to reduce unnecessary personal information.

Model answer and reasoning

Consider the school, pupils/staff, neighbours and the specialist using the observations. Reduce capture scope, choose a suitable time and restrict distribution; review/redact identifiable material where appropriate. Record the purpose and obtain the required advice/authorisations rather than assuming one person's permission resolves every interest.

Knowledge checks

Does technical ability justify collecting all visible information?

No. Collection should be proportionate to an established purpose.

Does flight permission settle privacy questions?

No. These are separate requirements.

pages.name: 02 · Make claims that match the evidence
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

02 · Make claims that match the evidence

Professional language distinguishes an observation, an interpretation and a conclusion requiring specialist competence. An image can show a visible feature; diagnosing its cause may require additional evidence or expertise. Avoid translating a strong visual impression into an unsupported engineering, medical, agricultural or legal conclusion.

Describe uncertainty specifically. State what was observed, the conditions, what was not observed and the effect on the decision. A limitation is useful when the reader understands what they can and cannot infer. Generic small print cannot repair a misleading headline.

Be equally accurate about credentials and tools. Completing a study course, holding a pilot credential, operating under a particular approval and possessing professional measurement competence are distinct claims. Cite evidence for each claim you make. Correct a material error promptly and preserve a version history so that earlier recipients can identify what changed.

Worked example

A thermal image contains a warmer-looking area. The report calls it an observed thermal anomaly under stated conditions, not a confirmed water leak or electrical defect without appropriate corroboration and interpretation.

Your exercise

Rewrite “our drone proves the roof is structurally safe” into an evidence-based statement for a visual observation service.

Model answer and reasoning

State that the service provides dated imagery of the agreed visible areas, identify observations and disclose coverage/visibility limits. Explain that structural safety requires assessment by an appropriately competent professional. The revised statement should not imply that absence of a visible defect proves safety.

Knowledge checks

Does absence of a visible defect prove safety?

No. The method has coverage and interpretive limits.

How should a material reporting error be handled?

Correct it transparently with a traceable version and communication to affected recipients.

Further reading / verification

  • Professional scope of service; FLIR measurement interpretation guidance

pages.name: 03 · Handle, share and retain data deliberately
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

03 · Handle, share and retain data deliberately

A data-handling plan identifies what is collected, where it is stored, who can access it, how it moves and when it is deleted or retained. Use the least access necessary for the task. Avoid sharing a general account or leaving a public link active simply because it is convenient.

Separate working files from approved deliverables. Check metadata and incidental personal information before sharing. A file may reveal more than the visible image through location data, names or attached records. The exact legal and contractual requirements depend on the project; identify the responsible people and current requirements before processing.

Plan for mistakes. If a link is sent to the wrong person, act through the organisation's incident process, preserve the facts and involve the appropriate privacy/security lead. Do not claim an incident is resolved merely because a link was disabled. Reassess retention and access at project close, including backups and outsourced processing arrangements.

Worked example

A team member proposes a public link to an entire project folder for one reviewer. A limited, time-bounded access arrangement to the relevant deliverables better matches the review task and reduces unnecessary exposure.

Your exercise

Create a data-flow map for a fictional inspection project, naming access roles, transfer points, retention decisions and an incident escalation owner.

Model answer and reasoning

The map covers capture media, working storage, processing services, review and delivery. It limits each role to necessary material, records external processors and explains review/deletion responsibilities. An incident path preserves evidence and refers decisions to the designated responsible personnel.

Knowledge checks

Can metadata disclose information beyond the picture?

Yes. Location, names and attached records may be included.

Does disabling a mistaken link finish incident handling?

Not necessarily. Follow the applicable assessment and response process.

04 · Resolve difficult requests and maintain accountability

Pressure often arrives as a plausible business request: remove a limitation, omit a missed area, make a qualification sound stronger or publish footage quickly. Identify the ethical issue before negotiating the delivery details. Explain the consequence in terms of the client's decision and the people affected.

Offer a workable alternative. A qualified report, a permitted recapture, a specialist review or a different framing can meet a legitimate need without making a misleading claim. If the request cannot be fulfilled responsibly, record the refusal and escalate through the agreed process. Professionalism includes saying no clearly and respectfully.

Build accountability into routine work through peer review, correction records, access review and reflective debriefs. Distinguish an honest error from an attempt to hide one; both require action, but the response should address the actual cause. Do not use a course exercise to name or accuse a real person. The capstone is a fictional decision record demonstrating your reasoning.

Worked example

A client asks the team to delete a documented coverage gap from the report. The team explains how that could mislead the recipient and offers an explicitly limited report or an authorised recapture, keeping the correspondence in the project record.

Your exercise

01 · Select a role using evidence of its work

Drone-related careers include piloting, data capture, processing, inspection interpretation, GIS, maintenance coordination and project delivery. A job title can combine several of these. Start with the actual tasks, outputs and accountability of the role rather than assuming a pilot credential covers the entire service.

Build a role-to-evidence matrix. For each requirement, identify a credential, work sample, supervised observation or other verifiable evidence that would demonstrate it. Separate mandatory authorisations from preferred tools. A useful gap statement describes what is missing and how you will demonstrate improvement.

Choose a focused initial direction. A broad list of interests is not yet a development plan. An inspection support role may require clear evidence handling and customer reporting as well as capture familiarity. A processing sample with documented quality checks can demonstrate different competence from a flight-hour log.

02 · Build a portfolio that can be verified

A useful case study explains the problem, your role, method, output, validation and limitations. State whether work was a client engagement, supervised exercise or simulation. The reader should be able to distinguish what you personally did from the team's contribution.

Protect confidentiality and permissions. Redact or replace sensitive locations, names and data where needed, and do not publish client material merely because you created it. A synthetic dataset can demonstrate a method without exposing a real project. Keep original evidence privately where the applicable agreements permit.

Include an accessible summary and a technical appendix suited to the role. Do not invent client outcomes, revenue improvements or accuracy claims to make a case study look more impressive.

Prepare interview stories that include tradeoffs, collaboration and correction of errors. Technical work often depends on recognising uncertainty and escalating appropriately. A clear account of a limitation can demonstrate judgement more effectively than claiming every project succeeded perfectly.

A development plan needs a target capability, practice activity, feedback source and evidence of progress. Course completion is one input, not the final measure of competence. Use a manageable review cycle. Record what you attempted, what the evidence showed and what to change. If a chosen resource does not address the gap, replace or supplement it. No. Appropriate performance evidence and assessment are still needed.

The next practice/resource based on the evidence of the actual gap.

01 · Prepare a station and a disciplined communication habit

Radiotelephony is a shared safety communication system. This course provides English ICAO-style rehearsal with South African source references; actual privileges, equipment, local procedures and examination requirements must be confirmed through the current SACAA/approved training process. The browser laboratory is a simulation and never transmits radio signals or grants a clearance.

Before a message, know who you need to contact, your identity, relevant position/state and the information or request. Prepare the message, listen to the channel and use deliberate, intelligible speech. Avoid rushing to sound experienced. Equipment setup, microphone technique and checks must follow the specific equipment and approved procedure.

Listening is an active task. Identify whom a message addresses and distinguish a restriction, an instruction, an acknowledgement and information. A message to a similar callsign is not automatically yours. If you have not understood the critical content, resolve it through the appropriate clarification rather than guessing. A simulator recording lets you review pacing and content without using a real frequency.

In the fictional lab, Dune Tower addresses Zulu Sierra Alpha Bravo Charlie. A message to a different training callsign is not adopted merely because part of the name sounds similar. The learner first identifies the addressee and the instruction.

Create a pre-message card with station, full training callsign, position/state, request and a listening/clarification reminder.

The card supplies enough context to prepare a concise message and explicitly checks addressee and understanding. It does not invent a real frequency or assume permission to transmit. The learner uses record/playback to inspect intelligibility and compares the content with the scenario.

Does the browser lab transmit radio signals?

No. It is a local communication rehearsal.

No. Resolve identity and ambiguity before acting.

02 · Spell identities with the phonetic alphabet

The phonetic alphabet gives letters distinguishable spoken forms. Practise the complete sequence: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu. Learn recognition as well as production; knowing the list in order is not enough when letters arrive unpredictably.

Work in short, variable groups before combining a complete identifier. Listen once, write the letters, check them and repeat the difficult combinations. Preserve the order and avoid substituting ordinary words that happen to begin with the same letter. In standard spelling, Alfa and Juliett use the internationally specified forms.

A correct alphabet recital does not make an incorrect identity correct. Associate the spoken letters with the actual scenario token and check the addressee. Do not abbreviate a callsign merely for convenience; actual abbreviation rules and initiation depend on the applicable procedure. The lab uses full training identifiers to keep identity clear.

Worked example

The token ZS-ABC is rehearsed as Zulu Sierra Alfa Bravo Charlie. The dash is a written separator, not another phonetic letter. A letter substitution changes the identity, even when the rest of the message is polished.

Your exercise

Spell ZS-KLM, ABC and JQX in a random order, record them and ask a partner to reconstruct the written tokens.

Model answer and reasoning

Expected groups include Zulu Sierra Kilo Lima Mike; Alfa Bravo Charlie; and Juliett Quebec X-ray. Compare the reconstructed letters, not only the speaker's confidence. Note any order or substitution error and repeat those groups with varied spacing and order.

Knowledge checks

What is the standard spelling for the A word?

Alfa.

Why practise random groups?

Real recognition requires identifying letters without relying on the alphabet’s sequence.

Further reading / verification

pages.name: 03 · Speak numbers, references and time without ambiguity
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

03 · Speak numbers, references and time without ambiguity

Digits and references carry meaning together. An altitude, a height, a pressure setting and a channel are not interchangeable numbers. Before speaking or reading back a value, identify what it refers to and the units or reference required by the applicable procedure. Never supply an omitted critical reference from your own assumption.

Practise individual digit recognition with aviation pronunciation, including tree, fower, fife and niner, while using the current local manual for the treatment of particular values. Decimal, level, pressure and time expressions follow their applicable conventions; do not transfer a convention from a different context without checking it. Written shorthand and spoken phraseology are related but not identical.

Use a two-column practice sheet: heard/spoken value and interpreted meaning. If the value is copied correctly but assigned the wrong reference, the communication has still failed. The laboratory's synthetic numeric prompts are spelling/listening exercises, not a source of current operational frequencies, altitudes or pressure settings.

Worked example

A fictional pressure-setting drill uses QNH 1018. The learner rehearses the digits and the QNH label, then distinguishes that pressure setting from an altitude. A separate numeric token is not silently interpreted as a clearance.

Your exercise

Prepare five fictional values, each with its type/reference. Have a partner read them; write both the value and its meaning before checking.

Model answer and reasoning

The sheet distinguishes number accuracy from interpretation. Errors include a wrong digit, an omitted reference or treating information as an instruction. Correct the item using the applicable manual and repeat with changed values; do not simply memorise one fixed phrase.

Knowledge checks

Is the right number with the wrong reference acceptable?

No. Meaning depends on both.

Does a lab numeric prompt provide operational information?

No. Values are synthetic practice tokens.

Further reading / verification

  • SACAA AIC 005/2018: transmission of numbers; current local procedures for levels/pressure/time

pages.name: 04 · Structure an initial call and a clear request
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

04 · Structure an initial call and a clear request

A structured message helps the recipient establish identity and context. In rehearsal, organise the station being called, your full callsign, the relevant position or state and the request. Actual content and sequence depend on the service and local procedure, so use the approved training framework rather than treating one mnemonic as universal phraseology.

Make the request specific enough to understand without adding irrelevant narrative. Prepare unfamiliar place names and important numbers. If a controller or station asks for additional information, answer the requested item clearly and retain identity as required. Do not convert a request into an assertion of permission.

Practise listening to the reply before rehearsing the next line. A scripted dialogue is useful for learning structure, but a fixed memorised sequence can hide a failure to understand a changed restriction. The lab varies fictional instructions and asks you to identify the critical elements. A good response reflects the actual message received, not the reply you expected.

Worked example

A fictional initial contact asks Dune Tower for information while stating Zulu Sierra Alfa Bravo Charlie and a defined training position. The model response is a communication example, not a real request to operate or enter airspace.

Your exercise

Write two initial-call rehearsals with different fictional positions and requests. Mark identity, state and request, then shorten unnecessary wording.

Model answer and reasoning

Both messages retain the addressed station and full training identity, give the relevant state and ask a specific question. They avoid invented operational permission, excessive storytelling and a memorised next line that ignores the station's actual reply.

Knowledge checks

Does making a request establish permission?

No. Request and authorisation are different.

What should change when the reply changes?

The response must address the actual instruction/information, not a fixed script.

Further reading / verification

  • SACAA AIC 005/2018: establishment of communication; approved local radio training examples

pages.name: 05 · Close the readback and hearback loop
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

05 · Close the readback and hearback loop

A readback gives the sender a chance to detect a misunderstanding. Identify the safety-critical instruction, values, restrictions and your identity. The applicable procedure determines what must be read back. An acknowledgement that a message was received is not automatically a readback of a clearance or restriction.

The sender's hearback is the other half of the loop. If the repeated content is wrong or incomplete, the discrepancy must be corrected. In practice, compare every critical element with the original rather than judging the confidence or speed of the voice. ROGER means received; WILCO indicates understanding and compliance, but neither should be used to replace a required specific readback.

The lab provides a critical-element checklist and a model response. Its text matching only highlights selected elements. It does not assess all phraseology, pronunciation, timing, context or safe decision-making, so it cannot award a radiotelephony pass. Review the complete exchange and, where possible, have a competent instructor assess the recording.

Worked example

In a fictional scenario, the instruction is to remain outside a named boundary and report at a stated point. The learner repeats the restriction and report point with the correct identity rather than answering only ROGER. A response implying entry would contradict the restriction.

Your exercise

Rehearse three lab readbacks. For each, list the critical items before speaking and compare your recording with the received message.

Model answer and reasoning

The worksheet retains identity, restriction and all relevant values/references. It identifies omitted or changed items and distinguishes a received-message acknowledgement from a complete required readback. A checklist match is recorded as practice feedback, not an instructor-approved pass.

Knowledge checks

Does ROGER replace a required specific readback?

No. It acknowledges receipt.

Can the lab’s token matching certify a radio response?

No. It is limited practice feedback, not a competence assessment.

Further reading / verification

  • SACAA AIC 005/2018: standard words/phrases and readback; instructor guidance

pages.name: 06 · Handle uncertainty, corrections and similar callsigns
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

06 · Handle uncertainty, corrections and similar callsigns

An unclear transmission is a reason to clarify, not an invitation to fill a gap. Identify the part you did not understand and request repetition or confirmation using the applicable phraseology. When you make an error in your own transmission, correct it explicitly so the listener can replace the wrong item rather than retaining two competing versions.

Be precise about standard words. SAY AGAIN requests repetition; CONFIRM seeks verification; CORRECTION introduces a correction. Do not use confident delivery to disguise uncertainty. If an instruction cannot be complied with, communicate that fact through the appropriate procedure rather than giving a misleading acknowledgement.

Similar identities and expectation can produce a persuasive but wrong exchange. Practise a scenario where the instruction is for another callsign, where one number changes and where a restriction is not as expected. Review what you actually heard and what you assumed. A polished script should never outrank the received message.

Worked example

The fictional lab gives an instruction to Zulu Sierra Alfa Bravo Delta while your token ends Charlie. The exercise asks you to recognise that it is not addressed to you, rather than perform a readback under the wrong identity.

Your exercise

Create a three-row error log: missed number, incorrect self-transmitted value and similar callsign. Give the appropriate clarification/correction objective for each.

Model answer and reasoning

The log distinguishes repetition of missed content, explicit correction of your own error and identity clarification. It records the original/incorrect/corrected items separately and avoids presenting guessed content as understood. Local phraseology remains subject to current manual and instructor review.

Knowledge checks

What is the risk in guessing a missing number?

A plausible guess can create an incorrect shared understanding.

What should happen after an error in your own transmission?

Make an explicit correction using the applicable procedure.

Further reading / verification

  • SACAA AIC 005/2018: repetition, correction and standard words/phrases

pages.name: 07 · Rehearse urgency and distress as fictional message planning
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

07 · Rehearse urgency and distress as fictional message planning

Distress and urgency communications have priority and specific procedures. The terms MAYDAY and PAN PAN identify different categories; learn their meaning and the current applicable message structure from the official manual and an instructor. In this course, practise only fictional planning and browser playback. Do not use real radio equipment or a live frequency for an exercise.

A useful emergency information plan keeps identity, the nature of the problem, intentions, position and other relevant information understandable. The exact sequence and required details depend on the situation and procedure. Do not invent a physical aircraft response from a communication exercise. For RPAS, distinguish an aircraft-system problem from the wider risk to people and other airspace users, and follow the applicable approved operational contingency.

Maintain the distinction between saying words and making an appropriate decision. The lab can help rehearse recalling information under a simple prompt, but it cannot assess whether an actual event is correctly classified or managed. Avoid dramatics and focus on intelligibility, facts and the information needed by those who can assist.

Worked example

A fictional tabletop prompt describes a serious problem and supplies an identity, position and intention. The learner builds a message from those facts, marks it TRAINING ONLY and checks the category/structure against the official reference with an instructor.

Your exercise

Complete a fictional emergency information card with identity, nature, intention, position/reference and relevant assistance information. State what remains to be verified by an instructor.

Model answer and reasoning

The card is factual and clearly simulated, does not invent a real location/frequency or aircraft procedure, and identifies the classification/phraseology for competent review. It separates communication planning from operational emergency actions and from a real competence assessment.

Knowledge checks

Does rehearsing an emergency message authorise live transmissions?

No. This is a fictional browser/tabletop exercise.

Does text matching evaluate emergency management competence?

No. Context, judgement and practical assessment require competent instruction.

Further reading / verification

  • SACAA AIC 005/2018: distress and urgency procedures; approved RPAS/operator contingency procedures

pages.name: 08 · Complete an integrated communication session and debrief
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

08 · Complete an integrated communication session and debrief

Combine preparation, listening, identity, number handling, readback and clarification in a short fictional scenario. Begin with a brief that defines the training callsign, station, role and information available. Use the browser voice as an optional prompt and your own recording for review; synthesised speech is not a model of a particular controller, accent or examination standard.

Record-and-playback is deliberately self-review. Listen for omitted restrictions, changed values, identity errors, unnecessary words and unclear pacing. A partner can reconstruct the message to test whether the intended information survived. The lab does not send recordings to a server or use automated speech recognition. Your browser and device control microphone permission and the recording remains a temporary local session object.

Finish with an error log and targeted next session. Repeat changed scenarios rather than one memorised response. Mark unresolved phraseology and local procedural questions for instructor review. A complete session portfolio demonstrates practice effort and corrected understanding; it does not confer a radio operator certificate or licence privilege.

Worked example

A session contains initial contact, a changed restriction, one missed value and a final readback. The learner identifies the change, asks for clarification and compares the corrected exchange with the model instead of treating an earlier expected reply as valid.

Your exercise

Complete six different lab scenarios, recording at least two. Build an error log, corrected responses and a plan for an instructor-reviewed session.

Model answer and reasoning

The portfolio shows scenario variety, checks the full message rather than token count alone and identifies concrete corrections. It records microphone/voice limitations and does not label the rehearsal a licensing pass. The next session targets remaining identity, number, restriction or pacing gaps.

Knowledge checks

Does the lab upload your voice recording?

No. The implemented recorder keeps a temporary object in your browser session.

What is the outcome of the capstone?

A self-study practice portfolio for review, not a radio certificate.

Further reading / verification

  • SACAA AIC 005/2018; current approved local practical radiotelephony assessment criteria

pages.name: Final project and assessment rubric
pages.html:
Authored self-study edition. Technical and instructor review pending. This is not approved practical training or a licensing qualification.

Final project

Complete a radio practice portfolio: phonetic reconstruction sheet, number/reference sheet, two initial calls, six varied lab responses, two record/playback reviews, one fictional emergency information card and a corrected error log. Obtain competent review before treating it as evidence of operational proficiency.

Assessment criteria

  1. Identity is retained and similar callsigns are noticed
  2. Numbers retain their quantity/reference
  3. Restrictions and required readback items are preserved
  4. Uncertainty is clarified rather than guessed
  5. Recordings and self-assessment are honestly limited

For each criterion, an instructor can award 0–20 points using the evidence below. A total is a course-work mark only; it does not grant an operational privilege, licence or practical competence finding.

  • 0–4: missing or materially misleading evidence.
  • 5–9: partial explanation; major gaps remain.
  • 10–14: relevant work with limitations/gaps to resolve.
  • 15–17: clear, traceable reasoning; minor corrections needed.
  • 18–20: complete evidence for this desk-based criterion, with assumptions and limitations handled accurately.

Self-review before submission: identify the evidence for each criterion, record unresolved questions and revise any unsupported claim. Do not invent a reviewer, approval or real-world outcome. The Assignment activity accepts an online-text portfolio for human marking after an instructor makes it available.

subjects.html:
DRAFT — STAFF REVIEW ONLY. Incomplete and unreviewed; not approved aviation training.

Air law and operating rules: opening lesson

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Separate sources, permissions and responsibilities.

Lesson

A reliable compliance decision identifies the jurisdiction, the type of activity, the applicable requirements and the evidence that each requirement is met. Begin with a proposed operation described in ordinary language. Identify who will operate, what aircraft is involved, where and when it will occur, and what the intended work is.

Separate pilot-related requirements from aircraft-related and operator-related requirements. A credential held by one person cannot by itself establish the status of an aircraft or an organisation. Likewise, agreement from a landowner does not establish the applicable airspace position. Keep evidence for these dependencies separately.

A current-source register is essential. Record document title, edition or amendment, relevant section, jurisdiction and the date checked. A search result, an old screenshot or another pilot's experience may identify a research lead, but should not silently become authoritative evidence.

When information conflicts, stop the compliance conclusion and resolve the discrepancy through the current authority material and competent training or operational personnel. Record what is known and what remains unresolved. This lesson intentionally supplies no numerical operating limits and does not claim complete regulatory coverage.

DRAFT — STAFF REVIEW ONLY. Incomplete and unreviewed; not approved aviation training.

Aircraft general knowledge: opening lesson

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Use configuration evidence and manufacturer instructions.

Lesson

Aircraft knowledge starts with the actual configuration. Record the aircraft identity, installed components, software versions, payload and applicable documentation. Similar-looking aircraft may have different capabilities or limitations. Avoid transferring a procedure merely because two systems share a brand.

Understand each system by function. Positioning estimates location; attitude sensing supports orientation estimation; the command link carries control and status; propulsion supplies force. A status indicator can describe one function without proving that the entire system is ready. Review the meaning of indicators in the correct manual.

Maintenance and fault decisions require evidence. Record symptoms and changes before replacing components or altering settings. Separate an observation from a proposed cause. A battery with visible damage requires the appropriate manufacturer and site process, not a live experiment intended to see whether it still works.

A configuration record should allow another competent person to identify which manual and limitations apply. This foundation supports later aircraft-specific lessons. It supplies no universal maintenance procedure, calibration sequence or emergency control action.

subjects.name: Principles of flight
subjects.html:
DRAFT — STAFF REVIEW ONLY. Incomplete and unreviewed; not approved aviation training.

Principles of flight: opening lesson

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Reason about forces with stated assumptions.

Lesson

Use a simplified multirotor model for this desk lesson. Weight acts downward. The aircraft's total thrust has a direction and magnitude. In a stationary level hover without other significant vertical effects, its upward component balances weight. This is an explanatory model, not a universal aircraft control setting.

When the aircraft tilts, the thrust vector tilts. Its vertical component becomes smaller if the total magnitude stays the same, while a horizontal component is introduced. Maintaining height while accelerating horizontally therefore requires an appropriate change in the total force balance. The flight controller's implementation depends on the aircraft.

Distinguish attitude, velocity and acceleration. Attitude is orientation; velocity describes motion; acceleration describes a change in velocity. A change in attitude need not produce the same immediate displacement in every environment. Wind and control response matter.

State assumptions before doing calculations. A diagram should name the aircraft type, axes, force directions and any effects omitted. Use the result to explain a concept, not to prescribe an unreviewed flight manoeuvre. Aircraft-specific performance and practical training belong in later reviewed lessons.

Meteorology: opening lesson

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Check the location and time represented by weather information.

Lesson

A forecast predicts conditions for a stated place and period. An observation records conditions at a reporting place and time. The crew's site observations add local evidence. Keep these source types distinct and record their coverage rather than treating them as interchangeable statements about the whole mission.

Terrain and structures can affect local airflow. A regional record may not describe flow near a particular ridge or building. Identify the gap and relate it to the planned operating area. Do not turn a general forecast into a guaranteed description of conditions at every point.

Information has both an issue time and a valid period. A newly downloaded document can still be old, and a recently issued product may describe a different future period. Check the actual metadata. Relate the evidence to aircraft limitations and the operation's reviewed procedures.

A decision log should record source identity, time, place, uncertainty, review points and the response to changing conditions. This lesson teaches information handling and decision quality. It does not supply numeric weather minima or replace locally applicable operational procedures.

subjects.name: Navigation
subjects.html:
DRAFT — STAFF REVIEW ONLY. Incomplete and unreviewed; not approved aviation training.

Navigation and flight planning: opening lesson

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Keep time, distance and reference frames consistent.

Lesson

Navigation calculations are meaningful only when units and reference frames are consistent. In a simple constant-speed ground-track example, time equals distance divided by ground speed. Two kilometres is 2000 metres; at 5 metres per second, the calculated travel time is 400 seconds. That result excludes acceleration, turns, wind changes, reserve and every other omitted mission factor.

Heading describes the direction the aircraft is pointed. Ground track describes its movement over the ground. Wind can make these differ. A map line alone does not establish the heading, energy or clearance required to follow it.

Coordinate-reference systems give numerical coordinates geographic meaning. Degrees of latitude and longitude are angular units, not metres. Changing a layer's label is different from transforming its coordinate values. A display that aligns layers cannot by itself validate a measurement workflow.

In mapping work, independent checkpoints are held out from the fitting or adjustment process so they can provide an independent check. Keep their role separate from control points. A planning note should identify units, horizontal and vertical references, the information omitted and the checks needed before applying a calculation to a real operation.

subjects.html:
DRAFT — STAFF REVIEW ONLY. Incomplete and unreviewed; not approved aviation training.

Human factors: opening lesson

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Make pressure and uncertainty visible in decisions.

Lesson

Human performance is part of the operating system. Workload, fatigue, attention and expectations affect how people interpret information and respond. A technically available aircraft does not establish that the crew is ready for the task.

External pressure can narrow attention. A client deadline, travel cost or desire to finish may encourage a person to dismiss contradictory evidence. Record the evidence and decision criteria before debating the commercial inconvenience of a delay. A stop decision supported by evidence can be a successful professional outcome.

Checklists support consistency, but reading words without checking the actual condition does not complete the purpose of a check. Clear role allocation and a shared understanding of intervention criteria help a team detect an omitted step or a mistaken assumption.

Use a debrief that separates observations from blame. Describe what happened, what information was available, what the team assumed and what process should change. Avoid inferring a person's medical condition or competence from a single error. The aim is a better decision system, with competent review where individual readiness is uncertain.

Communications: opening lesson

Objective

Resolve ambiguity before acting.

Lesson

Effective team communication makes the speaker, recipient, intended action and important conditions clear. In this desk lesson, use fictional crew roles and written messages. Operational radio phraseology, licensing and frequencies require current local references and competent instruction before practical use.

Ambiguity can arise from similar names, missing units, an unclear recipient or an unstated change of plan. A receiver should clarify uncertainty rather than choosing the most convenient interpretation. A response should demonstrate that the intended meaning was understood, not merely that a sound was heard.

Closed-loop communication includes a clear instruction or information item, an appropriate acknowledgement or readback, and confirmation or correction where needed. It is especially useful when a misunderstanding would have a material consequence. The exact required form depends on the approved procedure and context.

Keep operational records factual and proportionate. Record relevant changes and decisions without adding unnecessary personal information. After an unclear exchange, review the message structure and the team's process. Do not turn this general classroom model into a claim that a particular phrase is approved for live aviation radio use.
